lessons.plain: Every computer, from a phone to a giant server, does the same four jobs. Input is getting information in, like typing on a keyboard or a microphone hearing your voice. Processing is the computer working on that information, done mainly by the CPU (central processing unit), the chip that follows instructions. Output is showing or sending the result, like a screen, speaker, or printer. Storage is keeping information for later, like a drive that remembers files after power is off. Think of a kitchen: ingredients come in, the cook prepares them, a plate goes out, and the pantry keeps things for tomorrow.
lessons.guessPrompt: When you take a photo with your phone and it appears on screen and is still there tomorrow, which parts of the phone do you think handle getting the picture in, working on it, showing it, and keeping it?
lessons.teach:
The input-processing-output-storage cycle (often called IPOS) describes the four things any computing device does with data. Input is data entering the system; input devices include keyboards, mice, touchscreens, microphones, cameras, and scanners. Processing is transforming that data by following instructions; the CPU (central processing unit) does general work, and a GPU (graphics processing unit) is a specialized processor for images and parallel math. Output is presenting or sending results; output devices include monitors, speakers, and printers. Storage keeps data. RAM (random access memory) is fast, temporary working memory that loses its contents when power is cut, which makes it volatile. Long-term storage such as an SSD (solid state drive) or HDD (hard disk drive) is non-volatile, meaning it keeps data without power.

This model works because it lets you place any device or part into a role, which helps when you describe or fix a system.

Here is a worked example of a cashier scanning an item. The barcode scanner reads the code, which is input. The CPU looks up the price, which is processing. Along the way, the product list is read from the drive into RAM, which is storage. The price appears on the display and the receipt prints, which is output. The completed sale is written to the drive so it survives a reboot, which is storage again.

A common mistake is treating RAM and storage as the same thing because both are measured in gigabytes. RAM is short-term working space, and the drive is long-term keeping. Some devices also do two jobs: a touchscreen is both input and output, and a network card both sends and receives data.

In a running system, this difference matters. If unsaved work sits only in RAM when power fails, that work is lost. If a server runs out of RAM, it slows down badly even when its drive still has plenty of space.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic's receptionist photographs a new patient for their file. Trace the cycle: the webcam captures the patient's face, which is input. The CPU crops and resizes the image, which is processing. While it works, the image sits in RAM, which is temporary working storage. The finished photo shows on the monitor for approval, which is output. Missing step: the approved photo is then written to the computer's SSD so it is still there after the PC restarts tomorrow. Which role is this, and why?
choices: Storage, because the SSD is volatile working memory like RAM
Storage, because the SSD is non-volatile and keeps the photo without power
Output, because the photo is being sent somewhere outside the processor
Processing, because the photo is being changed into a saved file format
questions.why: Writing to the SSD is storage, and the SSD is non-volatile, so the photo survives the restart, unlike data held only in RAM.

questions.prompt: A technician says a laptop's memory is "volatile." What does that word mean here?
choices: It keeps its data safely even when the laptop is unplugged
It is the same thing as the drive, just measured in gigabytes
It loses its contents when the power is cut
It is a specialized processor for images and parallel math
questions.why: Volatile memory, such as RAM, is temporary working space that loses whatever it holds when power is lost.

questions.prompt: At a museum, visitors tap an information kiosk's touchscreen to choose an exhibit, and the same screen then displays a map to that exhibit. How should the touchscreen be classified in the input-processing-output-storage cycle?
choices: Both input and output, because it takes taps and also displays results
Processing, because it decides which map the visitor needs
Output only, because its main job is showing the map
Input only, because visitors touch it to make choices
questions.why: A touchscreen accepts the visitor's taps as input and displays results as output, so it does two jobs.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm's file server has 16 GB of RAM and a 4 TB drive that is only 20% full. During month-end, staff report that the server becomes extremely slow. A colleague says, "It can't be a memory problem, the drive has plenty of room." What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The server is running out of RAM, which slows it badly regardless of free drive space
The drive is too empty, so the server has nothing to read into RAM
The GPU is out of space, because it stores the firm's spreadsheets
Free drive space is used automatically as extra RAM, so RAM cannot be the cause
questions.why: RAM is short-term working memory and the drive is long-term storage, so a server short on RAM slows down badly even when its drive has lots of free space.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the four parts of the computing cycle using a device you use every day, and point out one case where a single component doesn't fit neatly into just one category or where the RAM-versus-storage difference causes a real problem.
lessons.modelAnswer: Every computer takes input, processes it, produces output, and stores data. On my laptop, the keyboard and webcam are input. The CPU follows program instructions to process that data, and the GPU handles graphics. The screen and speakers are output. Storage comes in two kinds. RAM is fast, temporary memory that empties when power is off. The SSD is slower but keeps files permanently. The model has limits, because some parts span categories. A touchscreen is both input and output, and a network card both sends and receives. The RAM-versus-storage difference also matters in practice. If my laptop crashes before I save, anything held only in RAM is gone. A server can also run out of RAM and slow down even when its drive has lots of free space, so you have to check the right resource.
rubricPoints: Names input, processing, output, and storage and gives a correct device example for each.
Identifies the CPU as the main processor.
Explains that RAM is volatile, temporary memory and that drives are non-volatile, long-term storage.
Notes that some devices, like touchscreens, serve more than one role.
Describes a real consequence, such as losing unsaved data or running low on RAM while disk space remains.

suggested.rationale: This is foundational vocabulary for classifying components, so it is best learned by reading and practicing recall rather than through any listed mission or engine.

lessons.plain: A notational system is a way of writing numbers using a fixed set of digit symbols. Everyday life uses decimal, which has ten digits, 0 to 9. Computers store everything as binary, which has only two digits, 0 and 1, because a circuit is either off or on. Writing long strings of 0s and 1s is tiring, so people use shorthand: octal, with eight digits, and hexadecimal, with sixteen. Think of it like measuring the same distance in inches, centimetres or feet. The amount never changes; only the way you write it down does.
lessons.guessPrompt: A network card's hardware address is printed as 3C:A9:F4:1E:07:B2. Why do you think it contains letters like A, B, E and F as well as numbers, and what kind of numbering might it be?
lessons.teach:
A notational system, also called a number base, is defined by how many distinct digit symbols it uses. Each position in a number is worth the base raised to a power, counting from zero on the right. This is called place value.

Decimal (base 10) uses 0 to 9, and its positions are worth 1, 10, 100 and so on. Binary (base 2) uses only 0 and 1, and its positions are worth 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. A single binary digit is a bit. Octal (base 8) uses 0 to 7. Hexadecimal, or hex (base 16), uses 0 to 9 and then A to F to stand for ten to fifteen.

Why this works as shorthand: one octal digit holds exactly 3 bits, and one hex digit holds exactly 4 bits, so you can convert by grouping bits without any arithmetic.

Worked example: take binary 11010110. For decimal, add the place values that have a 1: 128 + 64 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 214. For hex, split into groups of four from the right: 1101 and 0110. 1101 is 8+4+1 = 13, which is D. 0110 is 4+2 = 6. So the result is D6. Check: 13 times 16 is 208, plus 6 gives 214. For octal, split into groups of three from the right: 11, 010, 110, which gives 3, 2, 6, so 326. Check: 3 times 64 plus 2 times 8 plus 6 is 214.

Where you meet each one: binary is how hardware stores data. Hex appears in network hardware (MAC) addresses, memory addresses and web colour codes such as #FF0000. Octal appears in Linux file permissions such as 755. Decimal is used for everyday counts. Prefixes like 0b (binary), 0o (octal) and 0x (hex) mark which base is meant.

A common mistake is reading every number as decimal. Binary 10 is two, and hex 10 is sixteen. On a running server, misreading or mistyping an octal permission, such as 777 instead of 755, lets any user change the file, which creates a real security hole.

questions.prompt: A warehouse's barcode scanner logs one byte of status data as binary 10111001. A technician converts it to hex. Step 1: Split into groups of four from the right, giving 1011 and 1001. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: 1001 is 8+1 = 9. Step 4: Combine the digits to get B9. Check: 11 times 16 is 176, plus 9 gives 185, which matches the decimal sum 128+32+16+8+1 = 185. Which choice correctly fills Step 2?
choices: 1011 is read as the decimal number one thousand and eleven, which is too large for one hex digit
1011 is 8+2+1 = 11, which is written as 11 in hex
1011 is 8+4+2 = 14, which is E
1011 is 8+2+1 = 11, which is B
questions.why: The bits 1011 have 1s in the 8, 2 and 1 places, which add to eleven, and hex writes eleven as the single digit B.

questions.prompt: A junior developer at a game studio asks why hexadecimal (base 16) is such a handy shorthand for binary. How many bits does exactly one hex digit represent?
questions.why: Hex has 16 symbols, and 4 bits give exactly 16 combinations, so one hex digit always maps to a group of four bits.

questions.prompt: In a bakery's point-of-sale settings file, a value is written as 0x20. A new technician reads it as twenty. What is its actual value in decimal?
questions.why: The 0x prefix marks hex, so the 2 sits in the sixteens place: 2 times 16 plus 0 equals 32, not twenty.

questions.prompt: A library's file server stores a setting as binary 101011. An administrator needs it in octal (base 8). What is the octal value?
choices: 2B
questions.why: Grouping in threes from the right gives 101 and 011, which are 5 and 3, so the octal value is 53 (5 times 8 plus 3 is 43 in decimal, which confirms it).

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why engineers write numbers in hexadecimal or octal when the computer really works in binary. Include how to tell which system a number is in, and name one risk or limit of these shorthands.
lessons.modelAnswer: Underneath, the computer stores everything in binary, which uses only 0 and 1. Long binary strings are hard for people to read, so we use shorthand bases. A hex digit stands for exactly four bits and uses 0 to 9 plus A to F. An octal digit stands for exactly three bits and uses 0 to 7. This means you can convert just by grouping bits. For example, 11010110 becomes D6 in hex, 326 in octal and 214 in decimal. All four describe the same value. Context usually tells you the base: MAC addresses and colour codes are hex, Linux permissions like 755 are octal, and a prefix like 0x or 0b removes any doubt. The risk is ambiguity. The same characters, such as 10, mean two, eight, ten or sixteen depending on the base. Misreading the base, for example in a permission value, can quietly misconfigure a system.
rubricPoints: Binary uses only 0 and 1 because hardware stores data as off and on states.
Decimal is base 10, octal is base 8 with digits 0 to 7, and hex is base 16 with digits 0 to 9 and A to F.
One hex digit represents 4 bits and one octal digit represents 3 bits, which makes them compact shorthand for binary.
The value stays the same across bases; only its written form changes.
Context or prefixes such as 0x and 0b show the base, for example hex in MAC addresses and octal in Linux permissions.
Misreading the base, such as treating 10 as ten, is a common error with real consequences.

suggested.rationale: The exam asks learners to recognise which notation fits a scenario and to convert small values, so working through short exam-style situations builds that skill best, and no current mission covers it.

lessons.plain: Computers need units, just as a kitchen needs cups and minutes. Storage units say how much data something can hold. The smallest piece is a bit, a single 0 or 1. Eight bits make a byte. Kilobytes, gigabytes and terabytes are ever-larger piles of bytes. Speed units say how fast a processor ticks: megahertz and gigahertz count millions or billions of ticks per second. Throughput units say how much data a network moves each second, counted in bits per second. Think of a water tank: its size is storage, and how fast the pipe fills it is throughput.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your internet plan says 100 Mbps, but your download tool shows about 12 MB per second. Is something broken, or could both numbers describe the same speed?
lessons.teach:
A bit (binary digit) is one 0 or 1, the smallest unit of data. A byte is 8 bits, enough to store one simple text character. Storage sizes build on the byte. A kilobyte (KB) is about a thousand bytes. A megabyte (MB) is about a million bytes. A gigabyte (GB) is about a billion bytes. A terabyte (TB) is about a trillion bytes. Drive makers count in steps of 1,000. Operating systems often count in steps of 1,024, because 1,024 is a power of two. That difference is why a new 1 TB drive shows up as roughly 931 GB.

Processor speed is measured in hertz (Hz), meaning cycles per second. A cycle is one tick of the processor's internal clock. A megahertz (MHz) is a million cycles per second, and a gigahertz (GHz) is a billion. So a 3.5 GHz CPU ticks 3.5 billion times each second. Clock speed is only one factor in performance. The number of cores, the cache and the design of the chip also matter.

Throughput is the amount of data moved per second. It is measured in bits per second (bps), megabits per second (Mbps) and gigabits per second (Gbps). The case of the letter matters: a lowercase b means bits, and an uppercase B means bytes.

Worked example: how long does a 1 GB file take to download on a 100 Mbps link? Step 1: convert bytes to bits. 1 GB is 1,000 MB, and 1,000 MB times 8 is 8,000 megabits. Step 2: divide by the link speed. 8,000 divided by 100 gives 80 seconds, in ideal conditions.

A common mistake is treating Mbps and MBps as the same unit. They differ by a factor of 8. Someone who makes this error expects a backup or file transfer to finish eight times sooner than it really can. In a running system, that can mean missed maintenance windows, or links that turn out too small for the job.

questions.prompt:
A veterinary clinic uploads a 250 MB X-ray archive to its cloud storage over a 20 Mbps upload link. Estimate the upload time in ideal conditions.

Step 1: [missing step]
Step 2: Divide by the link speed: 2,000 megabits divided by 20 Mbps gives 100 seconds.

Which choice correctly completes Step 1?
choices: Leave the size as 250 megabits, because MB and Mb mean the same amount
Convert to kilobytes by multiplying: 250 MB times 1,000 gives 250,000 KB
Convert bytes to bits by multiplying: 250 MB times 8 gives 2,000 megabits
Convert bytes to bits by dividing: 250 divided by 8 gives about 31 megabits
questions.why: The file size is in bytes and the link speed is in bits per second, and each byte is 8 bits, so 250 MB times 8 gives the 2,000 megabits that Step 2 divides by 20.

questions.prompt: A laptop listing describes its processor as running at "2.8 ___", meaning its internal clock ticks 2.8 billion times each second. Which unit fills the blank?
choices: TB
GB
GHz
Gbps
questions.why: Hertz counts clock cycles per second, and a gigahertz (GHz) is a billion cycles per second. GB and TB measure storage, and Gbps measures throughput.

questions.prompt: An office manager installs a new drive labelled 2 TB. The operating system reports noticeably less than 2,000 GB of space. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The drive is faulty and has lost part of its capacity
The drive label is measured in bits rather than bytes
The operating system counts each byte as 10 bits instead of 8
The drive maker counts in steps of 1,000, while the operating system counts in steps of 1,024
questions.why: Drive makers count in steps of 1,000, but many operating systems count in steps of 1,024. The same number of bytes therefore shows up as a smaller number of gigabytes, with no fault involved.

questions.prompt: A small design studio pays for a 400 Mbps internet plan. Their download tool reports speed in MBps (megabytes per second). In ideal conditions, what is the highest speed the tool could show?
choices: 400 MBps
3,200 MBps
500 MBps
50 MBps
questions.why: Lowercase b means bits and uppercase B means bytes. A byte is 8 bits, so 400 megabits per second divided by 8 gives 50 megabytes per second.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how storage, processor speed and throughput are measured, and why mixing up bits and bytes causes problems. Name one limit of judging a computer by its GHz rating alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: There are three families of units. Storage counts bytes. A byte is 8 bits, and a bit is a single 0 or 1. The sizes go KB, MB, GB, TB, each roughly a thousand times bigger than the last. Some systems count in steps of 1,024 instead, which is why drives look smaller than advertised. Processor speed is measured in hertz, meaning clock cycles per second, so 3 GHz is 3 billion cycles a second. Throughput is network speed in bits per second: bps, Mbps, Gbps. The trap is that a lowercase b means bits and an uppercase B means bytes. To estimate a transfer, multiply the bytes by 8, then divide by the link speed. A 1 GB file on a 100 Mbps link takes about 80 seconds. GHz alone is a limited guide, because core count, cache and chip design also decide real performance.
rubricPoints: States that a byte is 8 bits and a bit is a single 0 or 1.
Orders the storage units KB, MB, GB and TB and notes the 1,000 versus 1,024 difference.
Defines hertz as cycles per second, with MHz meaning millions and GHz meaning billions.
Explains that throughput is measured in bits per second and that lowercase b means bits while uppercase B means bytes.
Shows the convert-by-8 step when estimating a transfer time.
Names a limit of GHz as a performance measure, such as core count or chip design.

suggested.rationale: The skill tested is picking the right unit and converting between bits and bytes in short scenarios, so reasoning through exam-style situations adds more than any current mission does.

lessons.plain: A troubleshooting methodology is a fixed, step-by-step routine for fixing technical problems so you don't just guess and poke at things. Think of how a doctor works: ask what hurts, look up similar cases, suspect a cause, run a test to check, give a treatment, make sure the patient actually recovers, then write it all in the chart. Following the same order every time saves effort, avoids making things worse, and leaves a written record so the next person who meets the same problem can fix it faster.
lessons.guessPrompt: A coworker says their laptop stopped connecting to Wi-Fi this morning. Before you change any settings, what is the very first thing you should do?
lessons.teach:
A troubleshooting methodology is an ordered list of steps for solving problems. The version CompTIA uses runs roughly like this. First, identify the problem: gather information, ask the user questions, note the symptoms (the visible signs that something is wrong), find out what changed recently, and try to reproduce the problem (make it happen again on purpose). Second, research a knowledge base (a collection of known problems and fixes) or the internet. Third, establish a theory of probable cause: your best guess at why it is happening, starting with the obvious. Fourth, test the theory. If the test confirms it, move on; if not, form a new theory or escalate (hand the problem to someone with more skill or authority). Fifth, establish a plan of action that fixes the cause with the least disruption. Sixth, implement the solution or escalate. Seventh, verify full system functionality: confirm everything works, not just the one symptom, and add preventive measures if you can. Last, document the findings, the actions taken, and the outcome.

The order works because each step narrows the possibilities before you risk changing anything.

Worked example: a user cannot print. You ask questions and learn that printing worked yesterday and that a system update ran overnight. You reproduce the problem by trying to print a test page, and it fails. A knowledge base article mentions updates that replace printer drivers. Your theory is a broken driver. You test it by checking the driver, and it does show an error. Your plan is to reinstall the driver after the user's meeting. You reinstall it, then print a test page and also check scanning. Finally you log the cause and the fix in the ticket.

A common mistake is to skip testing and jump straight to a fix, such as reinstalling the operating system. On a live system this can cause downtime, lose data, and still leave the real cause in place. Skipping documentation means the same problem costs full effort again next time.

questions.prompt: At a small bakery, the card reader at the till stopped taking payments this morning. You ask the owner questions and learn it worked at closing last night, and that the counter was cleaned and moved overnight. You run a test payment and it fails, so the problem is reproduced. The reader maker's support notes mention loose network cables. Your theory of probable cause is that the reader's cable came out of the router. MISSING STEP. The result confirms your theory. You plan to fix it before the lunch rush, plug the cable back in, run a test payment, check that receipts still print, and record the cause and fix in the shop's log. Which action fills the missing step?
choices: Write the loose cable in the shop's log as the cause of the problem
Escalate straight to the card reader maker before checking anything yourself
Look at the router port and cable to see whether the cable is actually disconnected
Replace the card reader with a new one so payments can start again quickly
questions.why: The missing step is testing the theory, which means checking whether the cable really is unplugged before you plan or make any fix.

questions.prompt: A technician at a city library has tested two theories about a failing self-checkout kiosk, and neither was confirmed. The technician decides to escalate. What does escalate mean in a troubleshooting methodology?
choices: Raise the ticket's priority so it is fixed today
Hand the problem to someone with more skill or authority
Restart the kiosk repeatedly until the fault clears
Reinstall the kiosk's operating system to rule everything out
questions.why: To escalate means to pass the problem to a person with more skill or authority, which is one option when a test does not confirm your theory.

questions.prompt: In a warehouse, the handheld barcode scanner app kept crashing whenever a worker scanned a pallet. A technician confirmed a corrupted app update was the cause and reinstalled the app. Scanning a pallet now works. What should the technician do next, before writing up the ticket?
choices: Check the app's other functions, such as syncing stock counts, and add preventive measures if possible
Close the ticket, because the reported symptom is gone
Form a new theory of probable cause about the crash
Search the knowledge base for other causes of app crashes
questions.why: After implementing a solution you verify full system functionality, which means confirming everything works and not just the one symptom, before you document.

questions.prompt: At a law firm, a technician fixed a shared calendar that would not sync, but wrote nothing down about the cause or the fix. Three months later the same fault appears, and a different technician has to work it out from scratch. Which step was skipped, and what did that cost?
choices: Documenting findings, so the same problem cost full effort again
Verifying full functionality, so the calendar never actually worked
Identifying the problem, so the symptoms were never recorded
Testing the theory, so the wrong cause was fixed
questions.why: Skipping documentation means the cause and fix are not recorded, so the next person must spend the full effort solving the same problem again.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, the troubleshooting steps in order and why the order matters. Include one limit or tradeoff, such as when you should escalate instead of continuing yourself.
lessons.modelAnswer: We follow a set order so we don't guess. First we identify the problem: ask the user what is happening, check what changed recently, and try to make the problem happen again. Then we research known fixes, form a theory about the likely cause, and test that theory before touching anything important. If the test fails, we form a new theory. Once a theory is confirmed, we plan the fix, carry it out, and verify the whole system works, not just the one symptom. Last, we document what we found, what we did, and the result. The order matters because changing things before we understand the problem can cause downtime or hide the real cause. The tradeoff is time: being thorough is slower. If a fix is beyond our skill or permissions, or the outage is costing too much, we escalate instead of experimenting.
rubricPoints: Names identifying the problem as the first step, including gathering information and asking what changed.
Describes forming a theory and testing it before applying a fix, with a new theory or escalation if the test fails.
Includes planning and implementing the fix, then verifying full system functionality.
Ends with documenting findings, actions, and outcomes.
Explains that the order prevents making things worse or missing the real cause.
Names a limit or tradeoff, such as time cost or knowing when to escalate.

suggested.rationale: This mission makes the learner run the full cycle on a real fault: identify a failing service, test a permission theory, apply the fix, restart, and verify the service works.

lessons.plain: A computing device is any machine that takes in information, processes it, and gives back a result. They come in different shapes because they serve different jobs. A smartphone fits in a pocket and is always connected. A tablet is a bigger touchscreen for reading and light work. A laptop is a portable full computer with a keyboard. A server is a powerful machine that serves many people at once. An IoT device is a small single-purpose gadget, like a smart thermostat, that talks to the internet. A gaming console is tuned for games and video. Think of vehicles: a scooter, a car and a delivery truck all move things, but each fits a different job.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small office wants one machine that stores shared files for all twelve staff and stays switched on day and night. Which kind of device fits best: a laptop, a tablet, or a server? Why?
lessons.teach:
A computing device is hardware that accepts input, processes it, stores data and produces output. On the exam, the skill is matching a device category to a need.

A smartphone is a handheld device with a touchscreen, cellular radio (connects through a mobile phone network), Wi-Fi, GPS and sensors. It runs a mobile operating system (the core software that manages the hardware), such as Android or iOS. A tablet is similar but has a larger screen and often no cellular radio. Both trade upgradeability for portability, because most parts are sealed in. A laptop is a portable general-purpose computer with a built-in keyboard, screen and battery. It runs a desktop operating system such as Windows or macOS, so it handles full applications. A server is a computer that provides services (files, websites, databases) to many clients, meaning the devices that request those services. Servers are built for reliability. They often have redundant parts such as two power supplies, and they run nonstop, usually in a rack (a standard metal frame) or in a data center. An IoT (Internet of Things) device is an everyday object with a small embedded computer and a network connection, such as a smart camera, thermostat or doorbell. It usually does one task, has little processing power, and is managed through an app. A gaming console is a specialized computer with strong graphics hardware, built for games and media streaming.

Worked example: a warehouse wants to track freezer temperatures remotely. First, the task is to measure and report one value, so it does not need a general-purpose computer. Second, the device must be small and always connected. Third, that matches an IoT sensor. The readings it collects would be sent to a server that stores them for many users.

A common mistake is picking a powerful desktop or laptop to act as a shared server. These machines are not built to run all the time or to serve many users at once. In a running office, that can mean files go offline whenever someone shuts the lid. Another risk is IoT devices left on default passwords, which become an easy way into the network.

questions.prompt:
A small accounting firm with 12 staff wants one shared place to keep client files. Everyone must be able to open those files at any time during the working day. Here is the reasoning, with one step missing.

Step 1: Many people will request the same files from their own computers, so this device provides a service to many clients.

Step 2: [missing]

Step 3: That matches a server, ideally mounted in a rack, rather than a spare laptop.

Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: It only does one task with little processing power, so a small embedded device is enough.
It needs strong graphics hardware so file previews appear quickly on screen.
It should be handheld with a cellular radio, so staff can reach the files from anywhere.
It must stay on all the time and keep working if a part fails, so redundant parts matter.
questions.why: Servers are chosen because they are built to run nonstop and reliably, often with redundant parts such as two power supplies, which a shared file store for many users needs.

questions.prompt: A delivery company wants each driver to carry a handheld device. It must show the driver's location on a map and let them call dispatch while they are on the road, far from any Wi-Fi. Which device category fits best?
choices: A Wi-Fi-only tablet
A laptop running a desktop operating system
An IoT sensor managed through an app
A smartphone
questions.why: A smartphone is handheld and includes GPS for location and a cellular radio that connects through the mobile phone network when no Wi-Fi is available.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits an IoT (Internet of Things) device?
choices: A specialized computer with strong graphics hardware, built mainly for games and streaming
An everyday object, such as a smart light bulb, with a small embedded computer and a network link
A computer in a data center that provides files, websites or databases to many clients
A portable general-purpose computer with a keyboard, screen and battery that runs full applications
questions.why: An IoT device is an everyday object with a small embedded computer and a network connection, usually doing one task and managed through an app.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic installs eight smart security cameras and never changes their factory default passwords. What is the main risk to the clinic?
choices: Attackers can easily log in to the cameras and use them as a way into the clinic's network.
The cameras will run out of processing power and need replacing with laptops.
The cameras will go offline whenever a staff member closes a laptop lid.
The cameras cannot work unless they are mounted in a standard metal rack.
questions.why: IoT devices left on default passwords are an easy entry point for attackers into the network they are connected to.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between a laptop, a tablet, a server and an IoT device for a given job. Name at least one tradeoff, for example portability versus upgradeability, or convenience versus security.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the job, not the device. If one person needs a full computer that can move with them, a laptop fits. It runs a desktop operating system, so it handles complete applications. If they mostly read, sign forms or browse, a tablet is lighter and cheaper. Smartphones and tablets trade upgradeability for portability, though: their parts are sealed in, so you replace them rather than upgrade them. If many people need the same files or service around the clock, that's a server. Servers are built for reliability with redundant parts, but they cost more and need a proper place to live, like a rack. If the job is one small task, such as reading a temperature or watching a door, an IoT device does it cheaply and stays connected. The tradeoff there is security: IoT devices are often weakly protected, so change default passwords and keep them updated.
rubricPoints: Matches the device to the task and the number of users, not just to raw power.
Identifies servers as always-on machines that provide services to many clients, built with redundancy.
Describes IoT devices as small single-purpose networked objects.
Distinguishes mobile devices (phone, tablet) from laptops by operating system and portability.
Names a real tradeoff such as portability versus upgradeability, or IoT convenience versus security.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this through short scenarios, so reasoning through which device fits which situation builds the skill best, and no current mission or planned engine compares device categories.

lessons.plain: A computer's insides are a team of parts, each with one job. The motherboard is the main circuit board that every other part plugs into, like a city's road system. The CPU (processor) is the brain that carries out instructions. RAM is short-term working memory that empties when the power goes off. Storage keeps your files after shutdown. An HDD stores them on spinning disks, an SSD uses memory chips with no moving parts, and NVMe is a faster kind of SSD. The NIC connects the computer to a network, and the GPU draws images and handles heavy math.
lessons.guessPrompt: A laptop has 512 GB of free drive space but slows to a crawl whenever you open thirty browser tabs. Which part do you think is running out: the CPU, the RAM, or the storage?
lessons.teach:
The motherboard is the main circuit board. It carries power and data between every other part and holds the sockets and slots they plug into. The CPU (central processing unit) executes program instructions. Its speed and core count decide how much work it can do at once.

RAM (random access memory) is fast working space for whatever is running right now. It is volatile, meaning its contents vanish when the power goes off. Storage is non-volatile and keeps data permanently. Storage comes in three main forms. An HDD (hard disk drive) reads magnetic spinning platters with a moving arm. It is cheap per gigabyte but slow. An SSD (solid-state drive) uses flash chips with no moving parts, so it is much faster and tougher. Many SSDs connect through SATA, an older cable interface that HDDs also use. NVMe is a way for an SSD to talk over PCIe, the motherboard's fast expansion lanes, which makes it several times faster than a SATA SSD.

The NIC (network interface card) gives the computer a wired or wireless network connection. It can be built into the motherboard or added as a card. The GPU (graphics processing unit) renders video and does massively parallel math for games, video editing and AI work.

Worked example: the tab-heavy laptop is slow. First check CPU use, which sits at 30%, so the processor is not the limit. Next check memory, which is at 98%. When RAM fills, the system starts swapping, which means it pushes overflow onto the much slower storage drive. Finally, the drive is an HDD, so swapping hurts badly. The best fix is more RAM. An SSD upgrade helps second.

A common mistake is mixing up memory and storage. Adding a bigger drive does not fix a RAM shortage. On a server, too little RAM causes constant swapping and slow responses, and a failed NIC drops the machine off the network entirely.

questions.prompt: A bakery's office PC takes about three minutes to start up and is slow to open saved order files. The technician works through it like this. Step 1: CPU use sits at 12%, so the processor is not the limit. Step 2: memory use is 35% of 16 GB, so RAM is not full and the system is not swapping (pushing overflow from RAM onto the slower storage drive). Step 3: ??? Step 4: The fix is to replace the drive with an SSD, ideally an NVMe SSD if the motherboard has spare PCIe lanes. Which choice is the missing Step 3?
choices: Check the NIC, because a slow network card makes local order files load slowly from the drive.
Check the storage drive: it is an HDD with spinning platters and a moving arm, so slow reads make it the bottleneck.
Since RAM is only 35% used, conclude the PC needs more RAM so memory fills up properly.
Check the GPU, because startup and file opening rely mainly on graphics rendering.
questions.why: With CPU and RAM ruled out, the slow startup and file opening point to the storage drive, and a spinning HDD explains it, which is why Step 4 replaces it with an SSD.

questions.prompt: A shop's tablet loses the half-written note it had open when the battery dies suddenly. The note's file had already been saved earlier, though, and that saved copy is still there after recharging. Which component held the unsaved, lost version of the note?
choices: The NIC, because it buffers open documents for the network
The motherboard, because it stores open files in its sockets
The SSD, because flash chips erase themselves whenever the power drops
RAM, because it is volatile and its contents vanish when power is lost
questions.why: RAM is volatile working space for what is running right now, so unsaved work in it is lost at power-off, while storage is non-volatile and kept the saved copy.

questions.prompt: A video studio wants the fastest possible drive for its project files in a new desktop. The motherboard has spare PCIe lanes, which are its fast expansion lanes. Which storage choice fits best?
choices: More RAM, because RAM keeps project files permanently
An NVMe SSD, because it talks over PCIe and is several times faster than a SATA SSD
An HDD, because it is the cheapest per gigabyte
A SATA SSD, because SATA is the fastest interface available for storage
questions.why: NVMe lets an SSD use the motherboard's fast PCIe lanes, making it several times faster than a SATA SSD and far faster than an HDD.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic's file server is still powered on and its local screen shows normal CPU and memory use, but every staff computer suddenly reports it cannot reach the server at all. Which failed component best explains this?
choices: The NIC, because it provides the network connection and its failure drops the machine off the network
The GPU, because the server cannot draw its desktop for remote users
The HDD, because a slow drive blocks all network traffic
The RAM, because a shortage causes swapping that makes the server unreachable
questions.why: The NIC gives the computer its network connection, so if it fails the server keeps running locally but disappears from the network entirely.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between RAM and storage, and when you would choose an HDD, a SATA SSD, or an NVMe drive. Name at least one tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: RAM is the computer's workbench. It holds whatever programs are running right now, it is very fast, and it is wiped when the power goes off. Storage is the filing cabinet. It keeps files permanently but is slower than RAM. If a machine slows down with many apps open, that usually points to a RAM shortage, not a full drive, because the system starts swapping overflow onto storage. For storage, an HDD uses spinning platters. It is the cheapest per gigabyte, so it suits bulk archives, but it is the slowest and the most fragile. A SATA SSD has no moving parts and is much faster, which makes it a good everyday upgrade. NVMe drives connect over the motherboard's PCIe lanes and are the fastest, so they fit the operating system or demanding work. The tradeoff is cost per gigabyte against speed.
rubricPoints: RAM is volatile working memory for running programs, while storage is non-volatile and keeps data permanently.
Running out of RAM causes swapping to storage, which a bigger drive does not fix.
An HDD is cheap and high-capacity but slow, because it has moving parts.
An SSD has no moving parts and is faster, and NVMe is faster still because it uses PCIe.
The tradeoff named is cost per gigabyte against speed or durability.

suggested.rationale: The unit's skill is picking the specific component behind a symptom or setup need, which is best practiced by reasoning through exam-style scenarios like the slow-laptop trace.

lessons.plain: Storage is where a computer keeps information. Some storage is volatile, meaning it forgets everything when the power goes off, like writing on a whiteboard that is wiped each night. Other storage is non-volatile, meaning it keeps data without power, like a notebook. Beyond that, storage can sit in different places. Local storage is inside or plugged into the device itself. Network storage lives on another machine in the same building and is shared over the local network. Cloud storage lives in a provider's data centre and you reach it over the internet. Each place trades off speed, sharing, cost and dependence on a connection.
lessons.guessPrompt: You are typing a report and the power suddenly cuts out. You had saved it ten minutes ago. Which part of your work do you think survives, and why might the last ten minutes be gone?
lessons.teach:
Volatile storage loses its contents when power is removed. The main example is RAM (random access memory), the fast working memory that holds programs and data the processor is using right now. Non-volatile storage keeps data without power. Examples are hard disk drives (HDDs, spinning magnetic platters), solid-state drives (SSDs, flash memory chips), USB flash drives and memory cards. Computers use both because RAM is very fast but temporary, while non-volatile storage is slower but permanent.

Storage also differs by location. Local storage is attached directly to one device, such as the SSD inside a laptop or an external drive plugged in by USB. It is fast and works offline, but only that device can easily use it. Network storage sits on the local network and is shared. A NAS (network-attached storage) is a box of drives that many computers open as shared folders. A SAN (storage area network) is a dedicated high-speed network that gives servers access to pooled disks, as though they were local. Cloud storage is kept by a provider in remote data centres and reached over the internet; you rent space, access it from anywhere and the provider handles hardware, but you need a connection and pay ongoing fees.

Worked example: you open a document from your laptop's SSD. Step one, the file is copied from the SSD (non-volatile, local) into RAM (volatile). Step two, your edits change only the copy in RAM. Step three, pressing save writes the copy back to the SSD. If power fails between steps two and three, the edits vanish with RAM, but the older saved version survives on the SSD.

A common mistake is thinking more RAM means more space to keep files. RAM does not store files permanently. In a running system, a server that relies on unsaved data in memory loses it on a crash or reboot, which is why important data is written to non-volatile, often network or cloud, storage.

questions.prompt: A bakery manager opens the shop's orders spreadsheet, which is kept on the shop's NAS (network-attached storage, a box of drives shared over the local network). Step 1: The file is copied over the network from the NAS drives (non-volatile, network storage) into the RAM of her office PC (volatile working memory). Step 2: She types in 40 new orders. These changes exist only in the copy held in RAM. Step 3: She clicks save. [MISSING: what happens at this step?] Step 4: Ten minutes later a power cut switches off her PC. When the power returns, she reopens the file and all 40 orders are there. What happens at Step 3?
choices: The updated copy in RAM is written back over the network to the NAS drives, which keep data without power.
The file is automatically moved to a provider's remote data centre over the internet.
The NAS copies its whole drive into the PC's RAM so both hold the same data.
The 40 orders are locked permanently into the PC's RAM so they survive the power cut.
questions.why: Saving writes the edited RAM copy back to the non-volatile NAS drives, so the orders survive when the PC's volatile RAM loses power.

questions.prompt: A technician is labelling parts on a workbench: a 2 TB hard disk drive, a 512 GB solid-state drive, a 16 GB stick of RAM and a 64 GB memory card. Which one is volatile storage?
choices: The 16 GB stick of RAM
The 512 GB solid-state drive
The 2 TB hard disk drive
The 64 GB memory card
questions.why: RAM is volatile, meaning it loses its contents when power is removed, while HDDs, SSDs and memory cards are non-volatile and keep data without power.

questions.prompt: A 12-person architecture firm wants every staff computer in the office to open the same project files as shared folders. They want a single box of drives kept on the office network rather than renting space from an internet provider. Which storage type fits best?
choices: A NAS, a box of drives on the local network that many computers open as shared folders
An external drive plugged into one designer's laptop by USB
A SAN, a dedicated high-speed network that gives servers access to pooled disks
Cloud storage kept in a provider's remote data centres
questions.why: A NAS sits on the local network and lets many computers open its drives as shared folders, which is exactly what the firm describes.

questions.prompt: A small cinema's ticket-booking server keeps the last hour of new bookings only in memory (RAM) and writes them to its drives once an hour. Thirty minutes after the last write, the server crashes and reboots. What is the result?
choices: The bookings from those 30 minutes are lost, because RAM is volatile and was never written to non-volatile storage.
Only the older bookings are lost, because new data in RAM is protected first.
The bookings are safe if the server has plenty of RAM, since more RAM means more permanent space.
All bookings survive, because a server's RAM keeps its data through a reboot.
questions.why: Data held only in volatile RAM vanishes on a crash or reboot, so anything not yet written to non-volatile storage is lost no matter how much RAM the server has.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between volatile and non-volatile storage, and then when you would pick local, network or cloud storage. Name at least one limit or tradeoff of each location.
lessons.modelAnswer: Volatile storage, mainly RAM, holds whatever the computer is working on right now and is very fast, but it is wiped when the power goes off. Non-volatile storage like an HDD, SSD or flash drive keeps data with no power, so that is where saved files live. Unsaved work in RAM is lost in a crash. For location: local storage, like the drive inside a laptop, is fastest and works offline, but it is hard to share and is lost if that one device fails. Network storage, such as a NAS for shared folders or a SAN for servers, lets many machines use the same data in the building, but it depends on the local network and someone has to maintain it. Cloud storage is reachable from anywhere and the provider runs the hardware, but it needs an internet connection and costs a recurring fee.
rubricPoints: Volatile storage such as RAM loses data when power is removed.
Non-volatile storage such as HDD, SSD or flash keeps data without power.
Local storage is attached to one device: fast and offline but not easily shared.
Network storage (NAS or SAN) is shared over the local network and depends on it.
Cloud storage is remote, reached over the internet, rented, and needs connectivity.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests picking the right storage type for a described situation, so reasoning through short scenarios builds that skill best, and no current mission or planned engine focuses on storage types.

lessons.plain: A peripheral is any device you attach to a computer to add a job it cannot do alone: a printer puts documents on paper, a scanner turns paper into a digital image, and a monitor shows what the computer is doing. The computer cannot use a peripheral until it has a driver, a small piece of software that translates the operating system's general requests into the exact commands that specific model understands. Think of the driver as an interpreter at a meeting: both sides are talking, but nothing useful happens until someone translates.
lessons.guessPrompt: You plug a brand-new printer into a laptop, the laptop says it found the device, but pages come out as pages of random symbols. Which piece is most likely wrong: the cable, the paper, or the software that tells the laptop how to talk to that printer?
lessons.teach:
Peripheral setup means connecting an external device, getting the operating system (the core software that runs the computer, such as Windows or macOS) to recognize it, and configuring it so it does its job correctly.

The key piece is the driver: model-specific software that converts the operating system's generic instructions, such as 'print this page' or 'scan at this quality,' into commands the hardware understands. Many systems support plug and play, meaning the operating system detects a newly connected device and installs a basic driver automatically. That basic driver often works but may lack features such as duplex (two-sided) printing or scanner color settings, so the manufacturer's driver is sometimes needed.

Printers may be local (attached directly to one computer, often by USB) or network printers (connected to the office network with their own network address so many computers can share them). Jobs wait in a print queue, a waiting list managed by the print spooler, the background service that feeds jobs to the printer one at a time. Scanners also need a driver plus scanning software to save the image. Monitors usually work with a generic display driver, but you set resolution (how many dots, or pixels, make up the picture) and refresh rate (how many times per second the image redraws), ideally to the monitor's native values; the graphics card's driver controls these.

Worked example: a new office network printer. First, connect it to the network and note its address from its control panel. Second, on the computer, add a printer and choose that address. Third, install the correct driver, ideally the manufacturer's version for this exact model and operating system. Fourth, print a test page. Fifth, set it as the default printer if most jobs should go there.

A common mistake is grabbing a driver for a similar model or downloading one from an untrusted site. The result in a working office is garbled output, missing features, jobs stuck in the queue, or even malware, so drivers should come from the manufacturer or the operating system's own update channel.

questions.prompt: At a small architecture studio, Priya connects a new monitor to her desktop. The monitor's specification sheet lists a native resolution of 2560 x 1440 pixels and a native refresh rate of 144 times per second (144 Hz). After she plugs it in, Windows shows a picture right away using a generic display driver, but text looks slightly blurry and the settings only offer up to 1920 x 1080 at 60 Hz. Step 1: She confirms the cable is firmly connected and the monitor is powered on. Step 2: She checks the spec sheet and notes the native values, 2560 x 1440 at 144 Hz. Step 3: ______. Step 4: She opens the display settings and selects 2560 x 1440 at 144 Hz. Step 5: She checks that text is sharp and motion looks smooth. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Choose the highest resolution currently listed, 1920 x 1080, and leave it there
Restart the print spooler service so the display settings refresh
Install the graphics card's driver from the manufacturer or the OS update channel
Download a driver made for a similar monitor model from a forum post
questions.why: Resolution and refresh rate are controlled by the graphics card's driver, so installing the correct one from a trusted source makes the monitor's native 2560 x 1440 at 144 Hz available to select.

questions.prompt: At a veterinary clinic, three staff members send documents to the same printer within a few seconds of each other. The printer prints them one after another without any job being lost. Which part of the computer system holds the jobs in a waiting list and feeds them to the printer one at a time?
choices: The scanning software, which saves images to disk
The print spooler, a background service managing the print queue
The plug and play feature, which detects new devices
The graphics card driver, which controls screen output
questions.why: The print spooler is the background service that manages the print queue and sends waiting jobs to the printer one at a time.

questions.prompt: A bookkeeper at a bakery plugs a new printer into her laptop by USB. The operating system detects it and installs a basic driver automatically, and a test page prints fine. However, the two-sided (duplex) printing option she needs for invoices does not appear. What is the best next step?
choices: Switch the printer to a network connection, because USB printers cannot print on both sides
Install the driver for a closely related model, since it will probably include duplex
Keep reinstalling the same basic driver until duplex appears
Install the manufacturer's driver for this exact printer model and operating system
questions.why: Basic plug and play drivers often lack features like duplex printing, and the manufacturer's driver for the exact model and OS supplies them.

questions.prompt: At a community library, a volunteer could not find the driver for a newly bought scanner, so he installed one from an unofficial download site that was labelled for a similar model. Which outcome is a realistic risk of this choice?
choices: Garbled or poor results, missing features such as color settings, or even malware
The monitor's refresh rate will drop because the drivers conflict
No risk, because any driver for the same brand works identically
The scanner will refuse to power on until the official driver is installed
questions.why: A driver for a different model or from an untrusted site can produce garbled output, missing features, or malware, which is why drivers should come from the manufacturer or the OS's own update channel.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a driver is and why a peripheral can be detected but still not work properly, including one tradeoff between relying on the automatic driver and installing the manufacturer's driver.
lessons.modelAnswer: A driver is model-specific software that translates the operating system's general requests, like 'print this' or 'scan at this quality,' into the exact commands one device understands. When you connect a printer, plug and play may detect it and load a basic driver, so the computer knows something is there. Detection is not the same as correct operation, though: if the driver is generic or for the wrong model, you can get garbled pages, jobs stuck in the queue, or missing features such as two-sided printing. The tradeoff is that the automatic driver is quick and comes from a trusted source but may be limited, while the manufacturer's driver unlocks full features but takes more effort and must be matched to the exact model and operating system and downloaded only from the manufacturer.
rubricPoints: Defines a driver as software that translates operating system requests into device-specific commands.
Distinguishes the device being detected from the device working correctly.
Names a symptom of a wrong driver, such as garbled output, stuck jobs, or missing features.
States the tradeoff between the quick basic plug-and-play driver and the fuller manufacturer driver.
Mentions getting drivers only from the manufacturer or the operating system's update channel.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine covers physical peripherals, so reasoning through exam-style setup scenarios such as a garbled printer or a blurry monitor best builds the skill of naming the specific component at fault.

lessons.plain: A device interface is the agreed way two pieces of equipment connect and exchange information, either through a cable and port or over the air. Think of interfaces like different kinds of doors in a building. Some doors fit delivery trucks, some fit people, and some only open when you tap a badge right against them. USB is the general-purpose door for plugging in accessories. HDMI carries picture and sound to a screen. Ethernet is a wired network link. Bluetooth is a short-range wireless link for accessories. NFC (near-field communication) works only when two devices are almost touching, as when you tap to pay.
lessons.guessPrompt: You tap your phone on a card reader to pay for coffee, and it works only when the phone is a few centimetres away. Why might designers deliberately make a payment connection work over such a tiny distance?
lessons.teach:
A device interface is a standard that fixes the connector or radio method, the signals, and the rules two devices use to talk. Knowing which interface fits a job is the skill tested here.

USB (Universal Serial Bus) is a wired standard for attaching peripherals, which are external add-on devices such as keyboards, drives and phones. It carries data and power. Connector shapes include the older rectangular USB-A and the reversible USB-C. Newer versions are faster.

HDMI (High-Definition Multimedia Interface) is a wired connection that sends digital video plus audio from a computer, console or streaming box to a monitor, TV or projector.

Ethernet is the wired standard for local networks. A cable with an RJ45 plug, an eight-pin connector that looks like a wide phone jack, links a computer's network port to a switch or router. It is usually more stable and faster than Wi-Fi because there is no radio interference.

Bluetooth is short-range wireless, typically about 10 metres, for accessories like headphones, mice and fitness trackers. Devices must first pair, which means they swap identity details once so they trust each other and can reconnect later.

NFC (near-field communication) is wireless that works only within about 4 cm. It is used for tap-to-pay, door badges and quick pairing. The tiny range is a security feature, because a person has to bring the device deliberately close.

Worked example: a new hire needs a desk set up with a laptop, an external monitor, wired network access and wireless headphones. Step one: video goes to the monitor, so use HDMI. Step two: a reliable network link is needed, so use Ethernet to the wall jack. Step three: the headphones are a nearby accessory, so pair them over Bluetooth. Step four: the badge reader at the door uses NFC.

A common mistake is treating Bluetooth and NFC as the same thing because both are short-range wireless. Bluetooth reaches across a room and keeps a connection going. NFC needs near-contact and is meant for brief taps. If you pick the wrong one, a design either fails to connect or exposes a payment or badge signal to people farther away than intended.

questions.prompt: A bakery is setting up a new checkout counter. Here is the plan, step by step. Step one: the handheld barcode scanner is an external add-on that needs both data and power from the till computer, so it plugs in over USB. Step two: the till must reach the back-office router reliably, without radio interference, so a cable with an RJ45 plug runs to the router over Ethernet. Step three: customers pay by holding their phone or card a few centimetres from the card reader, and the payment signal should not be readable from across the shop. Which interface does step three use?
choices: HDMI, because the card reader shows the payment amount on its screen
USB, because the card reader is a peripheral attached to the till
Bluetooth, because it is short-range wireless and keeps a connection going
NFC, because it only works within about 4 cm and needs a deliberate tap
questions.why: NFC works only within about 4 cm, so a customer must deliberately bring the phone or card close, which suits brief payment taps and keeps the signal away from people farther off.

questions.prompt: A warehouse supervisor buys a wireless barcode wand. Before it can work with her tablet for the first time, the two devices must swap identity details once so they trust each other and can reconnect automatically later. What is this step called?
choices: Pairing, done over Bluetooth
Patching, done over Ethernet
Mirroring, done over HDMI
Tapping, done over NFC
questions.why: Pairing is the Bluetooth step where devices exchange identity details once so they can trust each other and reconnect later.

questions.prompt: A hotel wants a streaming box in each guest room to send high-definition video and sound to the room's wall-mounted TV over a single cable. Which interface fits this job?
choices: Bluetooth, because the box and TV are in the same room
HDMI, because it carries digital video plus audio to a display
USB-A, because it is the older rectangular wired connector
Ethernet, because it is the most stable wired connection
questions.why: HDMI is the wired connection designed to carry digital video together with audio from a source device to a TV, monitor or projector.

questions.prompt: A gym designs its locker system so members unlock their locker from their phone over Bluetooth, the same way they connect wireless earbuds. What is the most likely problem with this design?
choices: The phone must be plugged into the locker with an RJ45 cable before it unlocks
An unlock signal could reach the locker from across the room, not just from someone standing right at it
The locker cannot receive power, because Bluetooth only carries data
Bluetooth only works within about 4 cm, so members would have to press the phone against the door
questions.why: Bluetooth reaches about 10 metres, so using it where NFC's near-contact tap belongs exposes the unlock signal to people farther away than intended.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between USB, HDMI, Ethernet, Bluetooth and NFC for a given device, and name one tradeoff, such as wired versus wireless or range versus security.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by asking what the connection has to carry and over what distance. If I'm sending video and sound to a screen, I use HDMI. If I'm attaching an accessory or a drive, or charging something, I use USB, which carries both data and power. For a network link that needs to be fast and steady, I use Ethernet with an RJ45 cable to a switch or wall jack. For a wireless accessory across a desk or room, like headphones, I use Bluetooth after pairing the devices once. For a quick tap, like payment or a door badge, I use NFC, which only works within a few centimetres. The tradeoff is that wireless is convenient but less reliable and easier to interfere with than a cable. Very short range, as with NFC, limits convenience but makes it harder for someone to intercept the signal or trigger it by accident.
rubricPoints: Matches HDMI to video and audio output to a display.
Matches USB to general peripherals, carrying both data and power.
Matches Ethernet to a wired network link using an RJ45 connector.
Distinguishes Bluetooth, which reaches roughly a room and needs pairing, from NFC, which needs near-contact.
Names a real tradeoff such as wired reliability versus wireless convenience, or short range improving security.

suggested.rationale: This objective is about recognizing standard connectors and wireless types, which is factual matching that reading and self-quizzing teach best, and no mission or planned engine covers physical interfaces.

lessons.plain: Virtualization means using software to split one physical computer into several pretend computers, each acting as if it had its own hardware. The software that does the splitting is called a hypervisor. Cloud computing takes this further: instead of owning the machines, you rent computing from a provider over the internet. Think of housing. On-premises is owning your own house and fixing everything yourself. Renting bare rooms is like renting raw servers. Renting a furnished flat means less to set up. Staying in a hotel means you just use it. Hybrid means keeping your house while also booking hotel rooms when needed.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small office wants staff to use email and a word processor through a web browser, with no servers to install or patch. Who do you think should be responsible for keeping that software updated: the office or the company providing it?
lessons.teach:
A hypervisor is software that lets one physical computer, the host, run several virtual machines (VMs), the guests. Each VM is a full simulated computer with its own operating system. A Type 1 hypervisor runs directly on the hardware with no operating system underneath, which makes it efficient and common on servers. A Type 2 hypervisor runs as an app on top of a normal operating system, like a laptop running a second operating system in a window. It works because most machines sit mostly idle, so sharing CPU, memory and storage among several VMs uses hardware better.

Cloud computing is renting computing resources from a provider over a network and paying for what you use. The service models differ by how much the provider manages. IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) rents raw virtual servers, storage and networks; you manage the operating system and everything above it. PaaS (Platform as a Service) gives a ready platform where you just upload your code; the provider handles servers and operating systems. SaaS (Software as a Service) is finished software you use, usually in a browser, such as web email.

Deployment models describe where things live. On-premises means the organization owns and runs the hardware in its own building. Hybrid combines on-premises systems with cloud services that work together.

Worked example: a team wants to run its own app without touching operating systems. Step one: do they want finished software? No, they wrote the app. Step two: do they want to manage servers? No. Step three: that leaves a platform that runs their code, so the answer is PaaS.

A common mistake is thinking cloud means the provider handles everything. With IaaS, you still patch the operating system. In a running system, assuming otherwise leaves rented servers unpatched and exposed to attack.

questions.prompt: A small bike-rental startup rents four virtual servers from a cloud provider. The provider supplies only the raw virtual machines, storage and network, and the startup installs and configures its own operating system on each one. Step one: what service model is this? The provider hands over raw virtual servers and nothing above them, so it is IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service). Step two: who is responsible for the operating system? ________. Step three: so when a security fix for that operating system is released, the startup's own staff must apply it, or the rented servers stay exposed. Which choice correctly fills step two?
choices: The startup, because with IaaS the customer manages the operating system and everything above it
Nobody, because virtual servers do not need operating system updates
The cloud provider, because anything running in the cloud is managed by the provider
The hypervisor, because it automatically patches each guest operating system
questions.why: With IaaS the provider manages only the raw infrastructure, so the customer (the startup) owns the operating system and must patch it.

questions.prompt: A university's IT team installs virtualization software directly onto a new rack server that has no operating system on it. They then create twelve virtual machines on that server. What kind of hypervisor are they using?
choices: A Type 1 hypervisor, because it runs directly on the hardware
A guest hypervisor, because each virtual machine runs its own operating system
A SaaS hypervisor, because it is delivered by a provider over a network
A Type 2 hypervisor, because it runs several virtual machines at once
questions.why: A Type 1 hypervisor runs on the bare hardware with no operating system underneath, which matches installing it on a server with no OS.

questions.prompt: An accounting firm pays a monthly fee so its staff can open a finished spreadsheet and document suite in their web browsers. The firm installs nothing and writes no code. Which cloud service model is this?
choices: IaaS, because the firm is renting computing resources
SaaS, because the firm uses finished software through a browser
On-premises, because the staff use it at their own office
PaaS, because the provider handles the servers and operating systems
questions.why: SaaS is finished software the customer simply uses, usually in a browser, with nothing to build or manage.

questions.prompt: A regional hospital keeps its patient-record servers in its own building, but also sends overflow website traffic to rented cloud servers, and the two systems are connected and work together. Which deployment model describes this setup?
choices: Type 2, because one system runs on top of another
Hybrid, because on-premises systems and cloud services work together
On-premises, because the hospital owns some of its own hardware
IaaS, because the hospital rents virtual servers for its website
questions.why: Hybrid means combining on-premises systems with cloud services that work together, which is exactly what the hospital does.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between IaaS, PaaS and SaaS, and where a hypervisor fits in. Name one tradeoff an organization faces when choosing between on-premises, cloud, and hybrid.
lessons.modelAnswer: A hypervisor is the software that splits one physical host into several virtual machines; Type 1 runs straight on the hardware, Type 2 runs as an app on an existing operating system. Cloud providers rely on this to rent out computing. The three service models differ by how much you manage. With IaaS you rent virtual servers and still manage the operating system, updates and apps. With PaaS you only bring your code and the provider runs the platform. With SaaS you just use finished software, like web email. The tradeoff is control versus effort: on-premises gives full control over hardware and data but you buy, house and maintain it all. Cloud cuts that work and scales quickly but you depend on the provider and an internet connection. Hybrid keeps sensitive systems in-house while using cloud for flexibility, at the cost of more complexity linking the two.
rubricPoints: Defines a hypervisor as software that runs multiple virtual machines on one physical host.
Distinguishes Type 1 (on hardware) from Type 2 (on an operating system).
Explains IaaS, PaaS and SaaS by how much the customer still manages.
Defines on-premises as owning and running your own hardware and hybrid as mixing it with cloud.
Names a real tradeoff such as control versus maintenance effort or provider dependence.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this by giving a scenario and asking which model or hypervisor type fits, so reasoning through situations builds the skill best since no mission covers it directly.

lessons.plain: A network is a group of devices connected so they can share information. A LAN (local area network) covers one small place, like a home or an office floor. A WAN (wide area network) links places far apart; the internet is the biggest one. Every device has two kinds of address. A MAC address is a fixed hardware name, like a person's name. An IP address is a changeable location, like a street address. Think of a building's mail room. The switch delivers mail between desks inside the building. The router sends mail out to other cities. The firewall is the guard who decides which mail is allowed through at all.
lessons.guessPrompt: In an office, two laptops on the same floor exchange a file, and one of them also loads a website hosted in another country. Which of those two trips do you think needs a router, and why?
lessons.teach:
A LAN (local area network) connects devices in one limited area, such as a home, classroom or office, usually owned by one organization. A WAN (wide area network) connects LANs across cities or countries, often over lines rented from a provider. The internet is a giant WAN.

Each device's network card (the NIC, or network interface card) has a MAC address (media access control address). It is a hardware identifier written as six pairs of hexadecimal characters, such as 3C:22:FB:1A:09:7E, and it is used only within the local network. An IP address (internet protocol address) is a logical address assigned by the network, such as 192.168.1.20 (IPv4) or a longer IPv6 form. It can change when the device moves, and it is what lets traffic find a device across networks.

A switch connects devices inside a LAN and forwards each packet (a small chunk of data) to the correct port by reading its destination MAC address. A router connects different networks, for example your LAN to your provider's WAN, and chooses a path by reading the destination IP address. A firewall inspects traffic and allows or blocks it based on rules, such as allowing web traffic and blocking unknown incoming connections. It can be a dedicated device or software on a computer. Home "routers" often combine all three.

Worked example: your laptop at 192.168.1.20 opens a website. First, the laptop sees that the destination IP is not on its LAN, so it sends the packet to the router's MAC address. Second, the switch reads that MAC address and passes the packet to the router's port. Third, the firewall checks its rules and allows outgoing web traffic. Fourth, the router forwards the packet onto the WAN toward the site's IP address, hop by hop.

A common mistake is treating a switch and a router as the same thing. A switch alone cannot reach the internet. In a running office, swapping a failed router for a plain switch leaves every desk talking to each other but cut off from the outside world.

questions.prompt: At a small dental clinic, the front-desk PC (IP address 10.0.0.12) sends a print job to the office printer (IP address 10.0.0.40). Both devices are plugged into the same switch on the clinic's LAN. Step 1: The PC sees that the printer's IP address is on its own LAN, so it addresses the packet directly to the printer's MAC address rather than to the router's. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: The printer receives the job and starts printing. The router never forwards this packet, because the traffic never leaves the LAN. Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: The switch reads the destination MAC address and passes the packet out of the port where the printer is connected.
The switch reads the destination IP address and sends the packet to the provider's network.
The firewall gives the printer a new MAC address so the packet can find it.
The router reads the destination IP address and forwards the packet onto the WAN toward the printer.
questions.why: Inside a LAN, the switch forwards each packet to the correct port by reading its destination MAC address, so no router or WAN is needed for local traffic.

questions.prompt: A technician checks a label on a warehouse barcode scanner's network card. It reads 7A:04:C1:9E:22:B0. What is this value?
choices: An IPv4 address assigned by the network
A MAC address, a hardware identifier used only within the local network
An IPv6 address that lets traffic find the scanner across the internet
A firewall rule that allows the scanner's traffic
questions.why: Six pairs of hexadecimal characters on a network card is a MAC address, a hardware identifier used only on the local network, unlike an IP address, which the network assigns.

questions.prompt: A law firm has one office in Leeds and another in Glasgow. Each office has its own LAN, and the firm connects the two offices using lines rented from a telecom provider. What type of network links the two offices?
choices: A single switched network, because switches read MAC addresses
A LAN, because one organization owns both offices
A WAN
A firewall, because the link carries private business traffic
questions.why: A WAN connects LANs across cities or countries, often over lines rented from a provider. Who owns the offices does not change that.

questions.prompt: A bakery's router fails. The owner replaces it with a spare plain switch and connects all the devices to it. What will most likely happen?
choices: Nothing works, not even local printing, because a switch only passes traffic once an internet connection is available.
The internet still works, but the bakery loses its firewall rules and all incoming connections are allowed.
The tills can still send jobs to the local receipt printer, but the online card-payment service cannot be reached.
Everything works as before, because a switch also chooses paths by reading destination IP addresses.
questions.why: A switch connects devices inside the LAN, so local traffic still flows. Without a router, nothing connects the LAN to the WAN, so outside services cannot be reached.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a switch, a router and a firewall each handle traffic differently, and how MAC and IP addresses fit in. Include one limit, such as what a switch cannot do or why one address type alone is not enough.
lessons.modelAnswer: Inside our office LAN, a switch connects all the desks and printers. It reads the destination MAC address, which is the fixed hardware ID on each network card, and sends the packet only to the right port. The switch has no idea how to reach anything outside the LAN.
