That job belongs to the router, which links our LAN to the WAN, meaning the provider's network and the internet. The router reads IP addresses, which are logical, assignable addresses that show which network a device is on. The firewall sits at that boundary and allows or blocks traffic by rule. The tradeoff is that strict firewall rules improve safety but can block legitimate apps until someone adds a rule. We need both address types: MAC handles the last local step, and IP handles finding the right network across the world.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes LAN as local and WAN as wide-area, linking networks such as the internet.
States that a MAC address is a hardware ID used within the local network.
States that an IP address is a logical, changeable address used to reach devices across networks.
Says a switch forwards within a LAN by MAC, while a router connects networks using IP.
Describes a firewall as allowing or blocking traffic based on rules.
Names a limit, such as a switch being unable to reach the internet or strict rules blocking legitimate traffic.

suggested.rationale: A virtual network path tracer would have the learner follow a packet through a switch, a firewall and a router, and say which address each device reads, which is exactly the identify-the-component skill this unit tests.

lessons.plain: A wireless network lets devices join a network using radio waves instead of cables. The rules for how that radio talk works come from a family of standards called IEEE 802.11, which most people know as Wi-Fi. Each newer version of the standard is generally faster and handles crowds better. Think of radio channels like lanes on a road. Some frequency bands have few lanes and lots of traffic, and other gadgets drive in them too. Other bands have many lanes but the road is shorter, because the signal fades sooner through walls. Choosing a standard and a band is a trade between speed, range, and how crowded the airwaves are.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your laptop's Wi-Fi gets slow every time someone runs the microwave in the next room. What do you think the microwave is doing to the wireless signal, and what might help?
lessons.teach:
IEEE 802.11 is the set of standards that defines Wi-Fi, meaning wireless local networking over radio. A frequency band is a range of radio frequencies. Wi-Fi mainly uses 2.4 GHz, which has longer range but is crowded, and 5 GHz, which is faster with more room but has shorter range and weaker wall penetration. Wi-Fi 6E adds a 6 GHz band. A channel is a slice of a band that one network uses.

The key versions, with theoretical maximum speeds: 802.11b, 2.4 GHz, 11 Mbps (megabits per second). 802.11a, 5 GHz, 54 Mbps. 802.11g, 2.4 GHz, 54 Mbps. 802.11n, also called Wi-Fi 4, uses 2.4 and 5 GHz, up to about 600 Mbps. 802.11ac, Wi-Fi 5, uses 5 GHz, reaching multiple gigabits per second. 802.11ax, Wi-Fi 6, uses 2.4 and 5 GHz (6E adds 6 GHz), up to about 9.6 Gbps, and is better at serving many devices at once. Newer versions are usually backward compatible, so older devices can still connect at their own lower speed.

Interference is unwanted radio energy or obstruction that weakens the signal. In 2.4 GHz, microwave ovens, cordless phones, Bluetooth gadgets, and neighbors' networks all compete. Walls, metal, and water also absorb signal. In 2.4 GHz, only channels 1, 6, and 11 do not overlap each other.

Worked example: a home office laptop on 2.4 GHz slows when the microwave runs. Step one, the microwave leaks energy near 2.4 GHz. Step two, the router's signal gets drowned out, so data must be resent. Step three, switch the laptop to the router's 5 GHz network, which the microwave does not touch, and the slowdown stops, provided the laptop is close enough for 5 GHz range.

A common mistake is treating the advertised speed as what you will get. Those figures are lab maximums shared among every device on the access point; real throughput is often far lower. In a running office, many users on one crowded channel means slow, dropped connections even with a newer router.

questions.prompt:
A dental clinic puts three Wi-Fi access points (the radios that devices connect to) in neighbouring rooms. All three use the 2.4 GHz band. The steps below are mostly worked out for you.

Step one: the technician checks the settings. The three access points are on channels 2, 3 and 4.

Step two: those channels overlap, so the access points interfere with each other. Data has to be resent, and connections slow down.

Step three: ______

Step four: the clinic's own access points stop interfering with each other, and connections improve.

Which action belongs in step three?
choices: Set all three access points to channel 6 so they match
Set the three access points to channels 1, 6 and 11
Raise each access point's advertised speed to 600 Mbps
Set the access points to channels 1, 2 and 3 so they are evenly spaced
questions.why: In the 2.4 GHz band, only channels 1, 6 and 11 do not overlap each other, so giving each access point one of those channels stops them from interfering with one another.

questions.prompt: A farm wants Wi-Fi in a storage barn that sits a long way from its router, with several walls in between. Only a few devices will connect, and they need only modest speed. Which frequency band (range of radio frequencies) is the best fit?
choices: 5 GHz, because it is the faster band
5 GHz, because it gets through walls better
2.4 GHz, because it has longer range
6 GHz, because it is the newest band
questions.why: 2.4 GHz has longer range than 5 GHz, and 5 GHz has shorter range and weaker wall penetration, so 2.4 GHz suits a distant spot that needs only modest speed.

questions.prompt: A coworking space installs an 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) router rated at up to about 9.6 Gbps. With 40 members online, each member measures only about 30 Mbps. What best explains this?
choices: The router must be faulty, because Wi-Fi 6 guarantees 9.6 Gbps to every device
Wi-Fi 6 works only on the 6 GHz band, so most devices fall back to 11 Mbps
Too few members are connected for the router to reach full speed
The rated speed is a lab maximum shared by every device, so real throughput is far lower
questions.why: Advertised Wi-Fi speeds are theoretical lab maximums that all connected devices share, so each user's real throughput is often much lower.

questions.prompt: A library still uses an old barcode scanner that supports only 802.11g. The library replaces its router with an 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) model. What happens when the scanner tries to connect?
choices: It connects at its own lower speed, at most 54 Mbps in theory
It connects only after the scanner is moved to the 5 GHz band
It connects at the new router's full speed of about 9.6 Gbps
It cannot connect, because 802.11g and 802.11ax are not compatible
questions.why: Newer Wi-Fi versions are usually backward compatible, so the older 802.11g device still connects, but only at its own maximum of 54 Mbps.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz Wi-Fi for a device, and name at least one tradeoff and one source of interference.
lessons.modelAnswer: Wi-Fi follows the IEEE 802.11 standards, and newer versions like 802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5) and 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) are much faster than older ones like 802.11b or g. The band matters as much as the version. 2.4 GHz reaches farther and passes through walls better, but it is crowded: microwaves, cordless phones, Bluetooth, and neighboring networks all share it, and it only has three non-overlapping channels, 1, 6, and 11. 5 GHz has more channels and higher speeds, but its range is shorter and walls weaken it more. So for a laptop near the router I would pick 5 GHz; for a device far away behind several walls, 2.4 GHz may stay connected better. I would also remember that advertised speeds are theoretical maximums shared among all connected devices, so real speed will be lower.
rubricPoints: Identifies 802.11 as the Wi-Fi standard family and that newer versions are generally faster.
States that 2.4 GHz has longer range but more congestion and interference.
States that 5 GHz is faster with more channels but shorter range and weaker wall penetration.
Names a real interference source such as microwaves, cordless phones, Bluetooth, walls, or neighboring networks.
Notes that advertised speeds are theoretical and shared among devices.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine simulates radio, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios about choosing a standard, band, or channel best builds the identify-the-component skill this unit requires.

lessons.plain: An operating system (OS) is the base software that runs a device: it shares out the processor, memory and storage among programs and lets people or other machines use the hardware. Different devices need different kinds. Phones and tablets run mobile operating systems built for touch and battery life. Personal computers run desktop ones built for one person at a keyboard. Servers run server operating systems that serve many users over a network around the clock. Gadgets like smart thermostats run tiny embedded systems that do one job. Think of vehicles: a scooter, a family car, a bus and a lift all move people, but each is built for its own job.
lessons.guessPrompt: A smart thermostat, a laptop, a phone and a machine that hosts a company's website all run an operating system. Which one do you think needs the smallest, most specialised operating system, and why?
lessons.teach:
An operating system (OS) is the software layer between hardware and applications. It schedules work on the processor, manages memory and storage, and offers an interface to users or other programs. Tech+ sorts operating systems into four categories by the device they serve.

A mobile OS, such as Android or iOS, runs phones and tablets. It is designed for touchscreens, saving battery, mobile networks and installing apps from a curated store, and it isolates each app for safety.

A desktop OS, such as Windows, macOS or a desktop Linux distribution (a Linux distribution is a packaged version of the Linux OS), runs a personal computer. It is designed for one user at a time, a graphical interface, and a wide range of applications and attached devices.

A server OS, such as Windows Server or a server Linux distribution, runs machines that provide services to many clients over a network. Clients are the devices asking for those services. It focuses on stability, many simultaneous connections, remote management and services such as file sharing, websites and user accounts. Often it has no graphical interface at all.

An embedded OS runs inside a dedicated device such as a router, smart TV, medical pump, car system or thermostat. It is small, fixed-purpose and often stored in firmware, which is software kept on a chip in the device. Some are real-time, meaning they guarantee a response within a strict time limit.

Worked example: a clinic needs software that controls an infusion pump. Step one: what is the device? A dedicated medical machine. Step two: how many jobs? One. Step three: are there strict timing needs? Yes. So the answer is an embedded, real-time OS.

A common mistake is to sort by brand name. Linux appears in desktop, server, embedded and, through Android, mobile systems, so always classify by the device's role. Choosing wrongly has real costs. A desktop OS on a busy web server may handle connections poorly, and an embedded device cannot simply be given a full desktop OS.

questions.prompt: A delivery company is giving each of its 40 drivers a handheld device. Each device has a touchscreen, must last a full shift on battery, connects over a cellular (mobile) network, and gets its route app only from an approved app store, with each app kept separate from the others. Classify the operating system. Step one: what is the device? A handheld touchscreen unit carried and used by one driver. Step two: [missing]. Step three: so the answer is a mobile OS. Which choice correctly fills step two?
choices: Its design needs are touchscreen input, saving battery, mobile networks, a curated app store and app isolation, which match what a mobile OS is built for.
The devices likely run Android, which is based on Linux, so they belong in the same category as a Linux machine.
Forty drivers rely on these devices, so the OS is serving many clients at once, which points to a server role.
Each device does one main job, running routes, so it is fixed-purpose and its OS should live in firmware.
questions.why: Classifying by the device's role and design needs (touch, battery, mobile networks, curated store, app isolation) is what identifies a mobile OS, not the number of users, a single app, or the brand underneath.

questions.prompt: An engineer says the OS in a car's braking controller is "real-time." In Tech+ terms, what does that mean?
choices: It updates itself from the internet as soon as a new version appears.
It guarantees a response within a strict time limit.
It can run many different applications at the same moment for several users.
It shows the current time and date on a graphical interface.
questions.why: A real-time OS is defined by its guarantee to respond within a strict time limit, which matters for devices like braking or medical controllers.

questions.prompt: A university department installs a machine in a rack with no monitor attached. It will store shared files and handle logins for about 300 staff laptops, and IT staff will manage it remotely. Which type of operating system fits this role?
choices: A desktop OS, because it supports a wide range of applications and attached devices
An embedded OS, because the machine sits in a rack and has no screen
A mobile OS, because the staff laptops are portable
A server OS, because it provides services such as file sharing and user accounts to many clients over a network
questions.why: A server OS is built for many simultaneous client connections, remote management and services like file sharing and user accounts, and it often has no graphical interface.

questions.prompt: A team labels the operating system in a smart thermostat as a "desktop OS" because they learn it is based on Linux. What is wrong with their reasoning?
choices: Linux is used only on servers, so the thermostat must run a server OS.
Thermostats are controlled from phones, so the thermostat itself runs a mobile OS.
They sorted by brand instead of by the device's role; a dedicated, fixed-purpose device like a thermostat runs an embedded OS.
Nothing is wrong; any OS based on Linux counts as a desktop OS.
questions.why: Linux appears in desktop, server, embedded and mobile systems, so the OS must be classified by the device's role, and a small fixed-purpose device like a thermostat uses an embedded OS.

lessons.explainPrompt: In your own words, explain to a teammate how to decide whether a device needs a mobile, desktop, server or embedded operating system, and name one tradeoff an embedded OS makes compared with a desktop OS.
lessons.modelAnswer: I classify by the device's job, not the brand name. If it's a phone or tablet, it needs a mobile OS like Android or iOS. That kind is built for touch, battery life and sandboxed apps from a store. If one person sits at it with a keyboard and many kinds of apps, it's a desktop OS like Windows, macOS or desktop Linux. If it provides services such as websites, files or logins to many clients over a network, around the clock, it needs a server OS like Windows Server or a server Linux. Those are tuned for stability, many connections and remote management, often with no graphical interface. If it's a dedicated gadget like a router or thermostat, it's embedded. The tradeoff with embedded is that it is small, efficient and sometimes real-time, but it is fixed-purpose. You can't install general apps on it, and updating its firmware is harder than updating a desktop.
rubricPoints: Defines an operating system as the layer that manages hardware for applications and users.
Classifies by the device's role rather than by brand, noting Linux spans several categories.
Gives a correct example and design focus for mobile, desktop and server operating systems.
Describes an embedded OS as small, fixed-purpose and often firmware-based or real-time.
Names a tradeoff, such as embedded efficiency versus lack of flexibility.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this by giving short device or task scenarios to classify, so reasoning through exam-style situations builds the skill best, and no mission or engine teaches the four OS categories directly.

lessons.plain: An operating system is the main software that runs a computer, and it is built from parts that each handle one job. A file system is the filing method that decides how files are named, stored and found on a disk. An interface is how you give the computer instructions, either by clicking pictures or by typing commands. Utilities are small built-in tools for upkeep, such as checking a disk or managing tasks. Drivers are translators that let the operating system talk to a specific piece of hardware. Think of a library: shelving rules, a front desk, a maintenance crew, and interpreters for visitors who speak other languages.
lessons.guessPrompt: You try to copy a 6 GB movie file onto an older USB stick that has 30 GB free, and the computer refuses. What do you think is stopping it, given that there is clearly enough space?
lessons.teach:
A file system is the set of rules an operating system (OS) uses to organize data on a storage device, including how big a file may be and who may open it. FAT32 (File Allocation Table, 32-bit) is an old, simple file system that almost every device can read, including cameras, game consoles, and Mac, Linux and Windows computers. Its key limit is that no single file can be larger than 4 GB. NTFS (New Technology File System) is the modern Windows file system. It allows very large files, sets permissions (rules about which users can read or change a file), offers built-in encryption, and keeps a journal, a running log of changes that helps it recover after a crash.

Worked example: you copy a 6 GB video to a USB stick formatted as FAT32. Step one, the OS checks the file size against the file system's rules. Step two, it sees that 6 GB exceeds the 4 GB per-file limit. Step three, the copy fails even though there is plenty of free space. The fix is to reformat the stick as NTFS, or as exFAT, a newer portable format. A common mistake is to assume that free space is the only thing that matters. File systems also cap individual file size, and FAT32 offers no permissions at all.

An interface is how a person controls the OS. A GUI (graphical user interface) uses windows, icons and a mouse or touch, and it is easy to learn. A command line interface (CLI) takes typed text commands. It is faster to repeat and can be scripted, meaning commands are saved to run automatically, but you must remember the exact commands.

Utilities are bundled maintenance tools, such as Task Manager, Disk Management, disk cleanup and backup. Drivers are small programs that translate between the OS and a specific hardware device. If a printer driver is missing or outdated, the printer may not work even though its cable is plugged in correctly.

questions.prompt: A bakery manager wants to keep a payroll spreadsheet on an external hard drive. Only her own Windows user account should be able to open it. The drive is formatted as FAT32 and has 500 GB free. The spreadsheet is only 2 MB. Here is the reasoning, with one step missing. Step 1: The requirement is a rule about which user may open the file, which is a permission. Step 2: FAT32 offers no permissions at all, so the current drive cannot enforce this rule. Step 3: ??? Step 4: Set a permission on the spreadsheet so that only her account can open it. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Run a disk cleanup utility to free more space so the permission settings have room to be stored
Split the spreadsheet into smaller files so that each one stays under FAT32's 4 GB limit
Install an updated driver for the external drive so that FAT32 gains permission settings
Copy the drive's data somewhere safe, then reformat the drive as NTFS, which supports permissions
questions.why: Permissions are a feature of the file system itself, and NTFS has them while FAT32 does not, so the drive must be reformatted as NTFS before Step 4 can work.

questions.prompt: A support technician at a shipping company must rename about 300 log files every night at 2 a.m., in exactly the same way each time, with no one at the keyboard. Which OS interface best fits this task?
choices: A graphical user interface (GUI), because its windows and icons make the task easy to learn
A device driver, because it translates between the OS and the storage drive
A command line interface (CLI), because typed commands can be saved as a script and run automatically
A backup utility, because it keeps copies of files before they change
questions.why: A CLI accepts typed commands that can be scripted, meaning saved to run automatically, which suits a repeated task with nobody present.

questions.prompt: A school office plugs a new barcode scanner into a computer. The cable is firmly connected and the port works with other devices, but the scanner does nothing. Which OS component is the most likely cause?
choices: A missing or outdated driver, the small program that translates between the OS and that specific device
The Disk Management utility, because the scanner has not been formatted
The file system, because the scanner's data is too large for FAT32
The command line interface, because the scanner needs typed commands before it can work
questions.why: A driver lets the OS talk to a specific hardware device, so if it is missing or outdated the device can fail even when the cable is connected correctly.

questions.prompt: At a dental clinic, a computer has suddenly become very slow. The office manager wants to see which running program is using the most of the computer's resources and close it. Which kind of OS component handles this?
choices: A driver, because it controls how the OS talks to the processor
A file system, because it decides who may open each program
A utility such as Task Manager, one of the bundled maintenance tools that come with the OS
The NTFS journal, because it logs every change made on the computer
questions.why: Utilities are maintenance tools bundled with the OS, and Task Manager is the one used to view running programs and end them.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why the company still formats some USB sticks as FAT32 when NTFS is 'better.' Explain the difference between the two file systems in your own words, including the tradeoff. Then briefly say when you would reach for a CLI instead of a GUI.
lessons.modelAnswer: A file system is how the operating system organizes data on a drive. FAT32 is old and simple, but almost any device can read it: cameras, TVs, consoles, Macs and Linux machines. The catch is that it can't hold any single file over 4 GB, and it has no permissions or journaling. NTFS is the modern Windows format. It handles huge files, lets you set who can open what, supports encryption, and recovers better after crashes because it logs its changes. The tradeoff is compatibility, since some non-Windows devices can't write to NTFS. So FAT32 makes sense for small files that need to move between many devices, and NTFS for Windows system drives and big files. As for interfaces, a GUI is easier for one-off tasks. I'd use a CLI when I need to repeat or automate something, because typed commands can be saved and scripted.
rubricPoints: Defines a file system as the OS's rules for storing and finding files.
States that FAT32 is widely compatible but limited to 4 GB per file and has no permissions.
States that NTFS supports large files, permissions, encryption and journaling but is less portable.
Contrasts a GUI (visual and easy to learn) with a CLI (typed, fast to repeat and scriptable).
Names the tradeoff of compatibility versus features or security.

suggested.rationale: The unit asks learners to name the exact OS component behind a given task, so reasoning through short exam-style scenarios, such as a failed large-file copy or a dead printer, builds that skill best.

lessons.plain: Most of what people do on a computer happens in application software, meaning programs that help a person do a task rather than run the machine itself. Exam questions usually sort these programs into four families. Productivity tools help one person make things, like documents, spreadsheets and slides. Collaboration apps help groups talk and work together. A web browser fetches and shows websites. Remote support tools let a helper see or control a computer from somewhere else. Think of an office building. Productivity tools are the desks. Collaboration apps are the meeting rooms and the mail room. The browser is the front door to the outside world. Remote support is the technician who can fix your desk without walking over.
lessons.guessPrompt: A help-desk technician in another city needs to see and click around on a user's Windows desktop to fix a crashing program. Which kind of software would let them do that, and how is it different from simply sharing your screen in a video meeting?
lessons.teach:
Application software is a program a person uses to get a task done. It sits on top of the operating system, which is the software that runs the computer itself. Tech+ groups common applications into four families.

Productivity tools help one person create and handle content. A word processor such as Word handles text documents. A spreadsheet such as Excel handles grids of numbers and formulas. Presentation software such as PowerPoint handles slides. Collaboration apps help several people communicate or work on the same thing. These include email, instant messaging or chat (Slack, Teams), video conferencing (Zoom), and shared online workspaces (SharePoint, Google Drive), where many people can edit one file. A web browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari) is the client program that asks web servers for pages over HTTP or HTTPS, the rules for moving web pages. It then renders those pages, which means it draws them on screen. Many productivity and collaboration tools now run inside a browser as web apps.

Remote support software lets a technician view or control a computer over a network. RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol) gives a full Windows desktop. VNC (Virtual Network Computing) shares a screen across different operating systems. SSH (Secure Shell) gives an encrypted text command line.

The grouping works because you can ask who the work is for and where it happens:

- One person making content: productivity.
- A group communicating or co-editing: collaboration.
- Reaching a website: browser.
- Fixing a machine you are not at: remote support.

Worked example: a remote user says the team budget keeps crashing.

1. The budget is a spreadsheet, so it is a productivity tool.
2. The team edits it together in a shared workspace, which is collaboration.
3. The technician must see the crash on the user's machine, so they open a remote support session, such as RDP, with the user's permission.

A common mistake is calling meeting screen sharing remote support. In a meeting, others only watch. Remote support also hands over control.

In a running system, remote access tools exposed to the internet are a frequent attack path. They need strong sign-in and limited access.

questions.prompt:
A community theatre's box-office manager says the ticket sales file is wrong. Classify each part of the job by asking who the work is for and where it happens.
Step 1: The sales totals sit in a grid of numbers with formulas, so the file is a spreadsheet, which is a productivity tool.
Step 2: Four volunteers update that same file at the same time in Google Drive, so the shared editing is collaboration.
Step 3: The theatre's ticketing website runs on a Linux server in another town. The IT contractor needs an encrypted text command line on that server to restart it. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Use a web browser, because the server hosts a website and the browser requests pages over HTTPS.
Use SSH, a remote support tool that gives an encrypted text command line on a machine you are not at.
Use RDP, because it gives a full Windows desktop of the remote machine.
Share the screen in a video conference so the contractor can watch the server.
questions.why: The contractor needs to fix a machine they are not at, which makes this remote support, and SSH is the remote support tool that gives an encrypted text command line.

questions.prompt: An office worker types a shop's address into Firefox, and the shop's home page appears. Which description matches what Firefox did?
choices: It let several people edit the same file at once in a shared workspace.
It acted as the client that requested the page from a web server over HTTP or HTTPS and then drew the page on screen.
It handed control of the worker's computer to a technician over the network.
It ran the computer itself and managed the hardware, as the operating system does.
questions.why: A web browser is the client program that asks web servers for pages over HTTP or HTTPS and then renders them, which means it draws them on screen.

questions.prompt: A help-desk technician works on a Mac. A user in a branch office runs Linux and needs help with a frozen program. The technician must see the user's screen and control it. Which tool fits best?
choices: A presentation program such as PowerPoint
An instant messaging app such as Slack
RDP, because it provides a full Windows desktop session
VNC, because it shares a screen across different operating systems
questions.why: VNC is the remote support tool that shares a screen across different operating systems, so it fits a Mac technician helping a Linux user.

questions.prompt: During a Zoom call at a dental clinic, a receptionist shares her screen to show colleagues an error message. A colleague says, "So she's giving us remote support." Why is that wrong?
choices: Zoom is a productivity tool, so it cannot share a screen.
In meeting screen sharing the others only watch, while remote support also hands over control of the computer.
Screen sharing is a web browser feature, not part of an application.
Remote support only works with SSH, so nothing else counts.
questions.why: Remote support lets a technician view and also control a computer, but in meeting screen sharing the other people only watch.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a given tool is a productivity tool, a collaboration app, a web browser, or remote support software. Name one place where the categories overlap or blur.
lessons.modelAnswer: I sort by who the work is for and what it does. A productivity tool helps one person make content: a word processor for documents, a spreadsheet for numbers and formulas, presentation software for slides. A collaboration app helps a group communicate or share work: email, chat, video conferencing, or a shared workspace where people co-edit files. A web browser is the client that requests pages from web servers over HTTP or HTTPS and renders them. Remote support software, such as RDP, VNC or SSH, lets a technician see or control a computer over a network. The categories blur in a few places. A spreadsheet in a shared cloud workspace is both productivity and collaboration, and many of these tools run inside a browser. Also, sharing a screen in a meeting is not the same as remote support, because remote support hands over control. That control is exactly why remote access must be locked down.
rubricPoints: Defines productivity tools as single-user content creation, with examples such as word processor, spreadsheet and presentation software.
Defines collaboration apps as tools for group communication or shared editing, such as email, chat, conferencing and shared workspaces.
Describes a web browser as the client that requests web pages over HTTP or HTTPS and renders them.
Describes remote support as viewing or controlling another computer over a network, naming RDP, VNC or SSH.
Names an overlap or limit, such as cloud apps spanning categories or screen sharing lacking control.
Notes the security risk of exposed remote access tools.

suggested.rationale: The unit's skill is matching a described task to the right software type, which is best practised by reasoning through short exam-style scenarios rather than by any existing mission or planned engine.

lessons.plain: A web browser is the program you use to open websites, and it comes with a few built-in tools that change how it remembers things. Private browsing opens a window that forgets your history, cookies and form entries when you close it. Add-ons, also called extensions, are small extra programs that give the browser new abilities, like blocking ads. A password manager stores your logins so you don't have to remember them. Clearing the cache throws away saved copies of web pages. Think of the browser as a desk: private mode is a scratch pad you shred afterward, and the cache is a pile of photocopies you can toss.
lessons.guessPrompt: You log into your email in a private browsing window on a shared library computer, then close the window. Do you think the library's network administrator can still see which websites you visited? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Private browsing (Chrome calls it Incognito, Edge calls it InPrivate) is a browser mode that does not keep local traces after the window closes. Local traces are your history (the list of pages visited), cookies (small files sites use to remember you), and form data. It does not hide you from the network: your employer, internet provider and the websites themselves can still see your traffic. Files you download also stay on the disk.

Add-ons, also called extensions or plug-ins, are small programs installed into the browser to add features such as ad blocking, translation or a password tool. They work because the browser lets them read and change pages. That access is also the risk. A malicious or abandoned extension can read everything you type, so install only from the official store and review the permissions it asks for.

A password manager is a tool, built into the browser or added separately, that stores logins in an encrypted vault (scrambled storage that only a key can unlock). It fills them in automatically, and many can generate strong unique passwords. Protect it with a strong master password or device lock, because anyone who unlocks it gets every login inside.

The cache is a folder where the browser keeps copies of images, scripts and pages so it can show repeat visits faster. Clearing the cache deletes those copies.

Worked example: a user says a company web page still shows yesterday's layout after an update. Step one: the browser loads its cached copy instead of fetching the new one. Step two: you clear the cache, or force a reload, which is often Ctrl+F5. Step three: the browser downloads fresh files, and the new layout appears.

A common mistake is believing private browsing makes you anonymous. Another is clearing cookies along with the cache without warning the user, which signs them out of every site. In a support setting, clearing cookies too can cost users their saved sessions, and an unchecked extension can quietly leak credentials.

questions.prompt: A hotel guest uses a shared lobby computer running Edge to check email and print a boarding pass. The goal is to leave nothing personal behind. Step 1: The guest opens an InPrivate window, Edge's private browsing mode. Step 2: The guest signs in to email and downloads the boarding pass PDF. Step 3: The guest closes the InPrivate window, and Edge throws away that session's history, cookies and form data. Step 4: ??? Which choice correctly completes Step 4?
choices: The guest should clear the cache so the email password is removed from the password vault.
Nothing else is needed, because closing the private window also removes the downloaded PDF.
The PDF is still saved on the disk, so the guest should delete it from the downloads folder.
Nothing else is needed, because private mode also hid the email traffic from the hotel network.
questions.why: Private browsing only discards local traces such as history, cookies and form data, so files you download stay on the disk until someone deletes them.

questions.prompt: An architecture firm's designers want a browser extension that translates supplier web pages. The extension asks for permission to read and change data on every website. What is the safest way to handle this?
choices: Approve it, because an extension can only change how pages look and cannot read typed text.
Use private browsing instead, because extensions cannot run in a private window.
Install it only from the official store, and check whether it really needs all the permissions it requests.
Install it from any download site, because all extensions get the same permissions anyway.
questions.why: Extensions can read and change pages, and that includes anything typed into them. So you should take them only from the official store and review what access each one requests.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic receptionist logs in to about 30 supplier and insurance websites and uses the same short password on all of them. Which browser feature best fixes this, and what must they also do?
choices: Private browsing, so the passwords are not stored on the computer after the window closes.
Clearing the cache each day, so old copies of the passwords are deleted.
An ad-blocking extension, so the sites cannot track which password is reused.
A password manager that generates and stores a unique strong password for each site, protected by a strong master password.
questions.why: A password manager keeps logins in an encrypted vault and can create unique strong passwords. Its master password must be strong, because anyone who unlocks the vault gets every login inside.

questions.prompt: At a warehouse, a technician fixes a stale inventory page by clearing the browser's stored data. Afterwards the shift supervisor complains that they have been signed out of the timesheet, email and shipping sites. What most likely happened?
choices: An extension was removed during the clean-up, and it had been holding the sign-ins.
The browser switched into private browsing mode, which blocks all saved sessions.
Clearing the cache always signs users out, because saved logins are kept in the cache folder.
The technician cleared cookies as well as the cache, and cookies are what sites use to remember a signed-in user.
questions.why: The cache only holds copies of images, scripts and pages. Cookies are what let sites remember you, so clearing them without warning signs the user out everywhere.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks when to use private browsing, extensions, the password manager and cache clearing for users. Explain each in your own words, including at least one limit or risk.
lessons.modelAnswer: Private browsing, like Incognito or InPrivate, stops the browser from saving history, cookies and form entries on this computer once the window closes. It's good on shared machines. Its limit is that it doesn't hide you from your employer, your internet provider or the sites you visit, and any downloads stay on the disk. Extensions add features like ad blocking, but they can read pages and keystrokes, so install them only from trusted stores and check their permissions. A password manager keeps logins in an encrypted vault and can create strong unique passwords. Its weak point is the master password: if someone unlocks it, they get everything. The cache stores copies of page files to speed up loading. If a site looks outdated or broken, clear the cache or force a reload. Be careful not to clear cookies too unless you mean to, because that signs the user out everywhere.
rubricPoints: Private browsing discards local history, cookies and form data but does not hide activity from the network or the websites.
Extensions add features but carry security and privacy risk because of the access they get to pages.
A password manager stores credentials encrypted and depends on a strong master password or device lock.
The cache holds copies of page resources for speed, and clearing it fixes stale or broken page displays.
Clearing cookies is separate from clearing the cache and logs users out of sites.

suggested.rationale: These are browser feature facts and support steps with no matching hands-on mission or planned engine, so reading and recall work best.

lessons.plain: Artificial intelligence (AI) means software that does tasks we normally link to human thinking, such as understanding a question or writing a paragraph. A chatbot is a program you type or talk to that replies in conversation. A virtual assistant is a chatbot that can also take actions for you, like setting a timer or sending a message. Generative AI creates new content, such as text or images, by predicting what should come next. Think of the phone keyboard that suggests your next word, scaled up enormously so it can write whole answers.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you type 'Peanut butter and...' into a text-writing AI, how do you think it decides what word to write next?
lessons.teach:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is software built to perform tasks that usually need human judgement, such as understanding language, recognising images, or making recommendations. Three everyday forms appear on the exam. A chatbot is a program that holds a text or voice conversation, often on a website to answer customer questions. A virtual assistant is a conversational program that can also act on your behalf, for example setting a reminder, playing music, or controlling smart lights when you speak a command. Generative AI is AI that produces new content, such as text, images, audio, or code, rather than only sorting or labelling existing content.

Most text-generating AI runs on a large language model (LLM): a program trained on a huge collection of example writing, called training data, until it learns which words tend to follow which. It works with tokens, small chunks of text that are often whole words or word pieces. Its core job is content prediction: given the text so far, it estimates which token is most likely next, adds it, and repeats.

Worked example. You type 'The capital of France is'. Step one: the model scores possible next tokens; 'Paris' scores far higher than 'banana'. Step two: it appends 'Paris'. Step three: it now predicts what follows 'The capital of France is Paris', perhaps a full stop. Step four: it keeps going until it predicts the answer is finished. No lookup in an atlas happened; the answer came from learned patterns.

A common mistake is believing the AI checks facts or knows the truth. Because it predicts likely-sounding text, it can produce a confident, fluent answer that is simply wrong. This is called a hallucination. In a running workplace, that means AI output must be reviewed before it goes into reports, code, or customer replies, and private or confidential data should not be pasted into public AI tools, since what you enter may be stored or used by the provider.

questions.prompt: A school office uses a text-generating AI tool (a large language model, or LLM, which writes by predicting the next small chunk of text, called a token) to draft parent notices. A staff member types 'Please remember to bring your'. Step 1: the model scores possible next tokens; 'lunch' scores far higher than 'volcano'. Step 2: ______. Step 3: it predicts what comes after 'Please remember to bring your lunch', perhaps 'tomorrow'. Step 4: it repeats this until it predicts the notice is finished. Which choice correctly fills Step 2?
choices: It appends 'lunch' to the text so far
It stops, because one predicted word completes its job
It checks the school timetable to confirm lunch is needed
It asks a teacher to approve the word before continuing
questions.why: Content prediction works by adding the highest-scoring token to the text and then predicting again from the longer text, with no lookup of real records.

questions.prompt: A hotel's website shows a pop-up window where guests type questions such as 'What time is checkout?' and get typed replies. It cannot book rooms or change anything for them. Which form of AI is this?
choices: A chatbot
A virtual assistant
A token
Training data
questions.why: A chatbot is a program that holds a text or voice conversation, such as answering customer questions on a website, without acting on your behalf.

questions.prompt: A bicycle shop's marketing team types a description into an AI tool and receives a brand-new poster image of a red bike on a mountain road that did not exist before. Which term best describes this tool?
choices: A chatbot
Training data
A virtual assistant
Generative AI
questions.why: Generative AI produces new content such as images, text, audio, or code, rather than only sorting or labelling content that already exists.

questions.prompt: A legal assistant asks a public AI tool to summarise a contract dispute. The fluent, confident answer cites a court case that turns out not to exist. What does this show, and what should the firm do?
choices: It is a token error; ask the same question again and trust the second answer
It is normal training data; the case exists but is private, so the answer can be filed
It is a hallucination; the tool checked a database that was out of date, so refresh it
It is a hallucination; review AI output before use and keep confidential data out of public tools
questions.why: Because an LLM predicts likely-sounding text rather than checking facts, it can produce confident wrong answers, so output needs human review and private data should not be pasted into public tools.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a chatbot, a virtual assistant, and generative AI, how generative AI produces its answers, and one limit they should keep in mind when using it at work.
lessons.modelAnswer: A chatbot is a program you talk to in text or voice, like the help window on a shop's website. A virtual assistant is a conversational program that can also do things for you, such as setting reminders or turning on lights. Generative AI is AI that creates new content, like text or images. Text tools usually run on a large language model, which was trained on lots of example writing. It works by prediction: it looks at the text so far, picks the most likely next chunk of text, called a token, adds it, and repeats until the answer is done. The limit is that it predicts plausible text rather than checking facts, so it can hallucinate, giving a confident but wrong answer. So we review its output before using it, and we keep confidential data out of public AI tools.
rubricPoints: A chatbot is a conversational program that answers in text or voice.
A virtual assistant converses and also performs actions for the user.
Generative AI creates new content rather than only sorting existing content.
Generative AI produces text by repeatedly predicting the most likely next token based on patterns from training data.
It can hallucinate confident wrong answers, so output needs human review.
Sensitive data should not be entered into public AI tools.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine exercises AI concepts, and the core skill is being able to distinguish the three AI types and describe prediction and its limits in your own words.

lessons.plain: A programming language is a way of writing instructions that a computer can eventually follow. Computers only understand machine code, which is raw numbers, so every language needs some kind of translation. Think of hiring a translator for a book: a compiled language translates the whole book in advance; an interpreted language uses a live interpreter reading aloud line by line. Scripting languages are interpreted languages used to automate everyday jobs. Markup languages do not give orders at all; they label content, like a highlighter marking headings. Assembly sits closest to the hardware, using short words that stand almost directly for the processor's own instructions.
lessons.guessPrompt: If one program is fully translated into a ready-to-run file before anyone uses it, and another is translated line by line every time it runs, which one would you guess starts and runs faster, and which one is easier to change and test quickly?
lessons.teach:
Machine code is the binary instructions a processor (CPU) actually executes. Every other language is translated into it somehow.

A compiled language, such as C, C++ or Go, is turned into machine code ahead of time by a compiler, a program that translates the whole source file into an executable file. The result runs fast because the translation is already done, but you must recompile after every change and usually separately for each operating system or processor type.

An interpreted language, such as Python or JavaScript, is run by an interpreter, a program that reads and executes the source code at run time, line by line. It is quick to edit and test and works on any machine with the interpreter installed, but it typically runs slower and needs that interpreter present.

A scripting language is an interpreted language used to automate tasks or glue programs together, such as Bash, PowerShell or Python. Scripts are usually short and run without a separate build step.

A markup language, such as HTML or XML, uses tags to describe structure and meaning of content, for example marking text as a heading. It has no logic like loops or decisions, so it is not a programming language in the strict sense.

Assembly language uses short mnemonics such as MOV or ADD that map almost one-to-one to CPU instructions. An assembler translates it to machine code. It is very fast and precise but hard to write and tied to one processor family.

Worked example: a team needs a nightly job that copies log files. Step one, it must automate a task. Step two, speed is not critical and frequent edits are likely. Step three, so a scripting language like Bash or PowerShell fits. A web page layout instead needs markup; a device driver squeezing every cycle might use assembly or a compiled language.

Common mistake: calling HTML a programming language. In a running system, forgetting that interpreted code needs its interpreter installed causes it to fail on a fresh server.

questions.prompt: A small game studio is choosing a language for the physics engine in its new racing game, which will ship on two different consoles. Step one: the engine runs thousands of collision calculations every frame, so speed is critical. Step two: [missing]. Step three: so a compiled language such as C++ fits, translated ahead of time into a separate executable for each console. Which statement best fills step two?
choices: The engine mainly needs tags that describe the structure of its menus and headings.
The engine will be edited constantly, so changes must run immediately without any build step.
Doing the translation ahead of time is worth the cost of a separate build for each console after every change.
The engine must run on any machine that has an interpreter installed, so no build step is needed.
questions.why: A compiled language trades a recompile for every change and every processor or operating system for fast-running machine code, and that trade suits a speed-critical engine.

questions.prompt: A charity's web designer says she is a programmer because she writes XML files that use tags to label each donor record's name, address and gift amount. Based on how languages are classified, what is the most accurate description of XML?
choices: A markup language that describes the structure and meaning of content but has no loops or decisions, so it is not a programming language in the strict sense.
A scripting language, because XML files are short and run without a separate build step.
A compiled language, because a compiler turns the tags into an executable file.
An assembly language, because each tag maps almost one-to-one to a CPU instruction.
questions.why: XML uses tags to describe content and contains no logic such as loops or decisions, which makes it markup rather than a programming language.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's analyst writes a Python program that runs perfectly on his laptop. The operations team copies only the .py source file to a brand-new server, and the program will not run there. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The server uses a different processor family, and Python code is tied to a single processor family like assembly.
The server has no Python interpreter installed, and interpreted code needs the interpreter present to read and execute it.
The program was never compiled into machine code, and Python programs must always be compiled before they can run.
The .py file contains tags instead of logic, so the server reads it as markup.
questions.why: Interpreted code is executed at run time by an interpreter, so a fresh server without that interpreter cannot run it.

questions.prompt: An engineer at a sensor manufacturer writes a routine using short instructions such as MOV and ADD, each matching almost exactly one instruction for the chip in the company's sensor. Which statement about this code is correct?
choices: It is a markup language, so a browser displays it rather than a processor running it.
It is an interpreted language, so it will run unchanged on any processor that has an interpreter installed.
It is already machine code, so it needs no translation before the processor executes it.
It is assembly language, translated to machine code by an assembler, and it would generally need rewriting to run on a different processor family.
questions.why: Mnemonics like MOV and ADD that map nearly one-to-one to CPU instructions define assembly language, which an assembler translates and which is tied to one processor family.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between compiled, interpreted, scripting, markup and assembly languages, and name one tradeoff between compiled and interpreted code.
lessons.modelAnswer: Computers only run machine code, so languages differ mainly in how they get translated. A compiled language like C is translated in advance by a compiler into an executable file; it runs fast, but every change means recompiling, often once per platform. An interpreted language like Python is read and run line by line by an interpreter at run time; it is easy to change and portable, but slower and the interpreter must be installed. Scripting languages such as Bash or PowerShell are interpreted languages used to automate tasks. Markup languages like HTML only label structure with tags and contain no logic, so they are not really programming languages. Assembly uses mnemonics that map nearly one-to-one to CPU instructions, so it is very fast but hard to write and tied to one processor family.
rubricPoints: Compiled code is translated ahead of time into an executable by a compiler and runs fast.
Interpreted code is executed line by line at run time and needs an interpreter present.
Scripting languages are interpreted languages used to automate tasks.
Markup languages describe structure with tags and have no program logic.
Assembly uses mnemonics close to CPU instructions and is processor-specific.
Names a tradeoff such as speed versus ease of change or portability.

suggested.rationale: The exam asks learners to match a described situation to the right language category, so reasoning through short scenarios builds that skill better than any single hands-on mission.

lessons.plain: A data type is a label that tells the computer what kind of value it is holding, so it knows how to store that value and what it can do with it. Think of a kitchen with labelled containers: you would not pour soup into an egg carton. A char holds one single character, like the letter A. A string holds a run of characters, like a name or a sentence. Integers are whole numbers, like 42. Floats are numbers with a decimal part, like 3.75. A Boolean holds only true or false, like a light switch that is either on or off.
lessons.guessPrompt: A sign-up form asks for a person's first initial, their full name, their age in years, their height in metres, and whether they want a newsletter (yes or no). Which kind of value do you think each answer is, and why might it matter which one the program uses?
lessons.teach:
A data type is the category a value belongs to. It tells the program how much memory to use and which operations make sense. There are five basic types to know.

A char (character) is exactly one letter, digit, or symbol, such as 'J' or '7'. A string is an ordered sequence of characters, such as "Jordan" or "Hello, world"; it is text. An integer is a whole number with no fractional part, positive or negative, such as 34 or -2. A float (floating-point number) is a number that can have a decimal part, such as 1.75; computers store floats as close approximations, so tiny rounding errors can appear. A Boolean has only two possible values, true or false, and is used for yes/no decisions.

Why types matter: the same symbols behave differently depending on type. Trace this example. If a program adds the integers 5 and 5, it does arithmetic and gets 10. If it adds the strings "5" and "5", most languages join (concatenate) the text and get "55". Same keys typed, different result, purely because of type.

Applying this to the sign-up form: first initial 'J' is a char; full name "Jordan Lee" is a string; age 34 is an integer because ages are counted in whole years; height 1.75 is a float because it needs a decimal; newsletter opt-in is a Boolean, true or false.

A common mistake is storing things that look like numbers but are really labels, such as phone numbers or ZIP codes, as integers. The ZIP code 02134 stored as an integer becomes 2134 because leading zeros are dropped, and nobody ever does math on a ZIP code. These belong in strings. In a running system, choosing the wrong type causes quiet damage: lost leading zeros, text joined instead of added, or rounding errors when floats are used carelessly for exact amounts like money totals.

questions.prompt: A pet clinic is designing a record for each animal it treats. Most of the fields have already been given types. The vaccine status letter, such as 'A', is a char because it is exactly one symbol. The pet's name, such as "Biscuit", is a string because it is text. The number of visits this year, such as 6, is an integer because visits are counted in whole numbers. The pet's weight, such as 12.4 kg, is a float because it needs a decimal part. Whether the owner agreed to reminder texts is a Boolean because the answer is only yes or no. One field is missing a type: the microchip number, such as 00981. Nobody ever does math on it, and it must keep its leading zeros. Which type should the microchip number use?
choices: Float, because a large number may need extra precision
Char, because each digit is a single character
Integer, because it is made only of digits
String, because it is a label made of characters and its leading zeros must be kept
questions.why: The microchip number is a label that nobody does math on, and an integer would drop its leading zeros, so it belongs in a string.

questions.prompt: A data type is the category a value belongs to. A char (character) is exactly one letter, digit, or symbol. Which of these values is a char?
choices: true
questions.why: 'Q' is exactly one letter. "Q1" is a string of two characters, 3.0 is a float, and true is a Boolean.

questions.prompt: A bakery's order app has two text boxes for quantities. A customer types 12 in one box and 8 in the other, and the app shows a total of 128 instead of 20. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The quantities were stored as strings, so the app joined (concatenated) the text instead of adding the numbers
The quantities were stored as floats, which caused a rounding error
The quantities were stored as integers, which always join text together
The quantities were stored as Booleans, which can only hold true or false
questions.why: Adding the strings "12" and "8" joins the text into "128". Adding them as integers would do arithmetic and give 20.

questions.prompt: A parking garage system adds up thousands of parking fees. Each fee, such as 3.10, is stored as a float (a number that can have a decimal part). At the end of the month, the total is off by a tiny fraction of a cent. What best explains this?
choices: Floats drop leading zeros, so some fees were shortened
Floats are stored as close approximations, so tiny rounding errors build up when they are used for exact amounts like money
Floats are joined like text, so the fees were concatenated instead of added
Floats cannot hold negative numbers, so refunds were lost
questions.why: Computers store floats as close approximations, so using them carelessly for exact amounts like money totals can cause small rounding errors.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between char, string, integer, float, and Boolean for a piece of data, and describe one limit or tradeoff of a type, such as what goes wrong if you store a ZIP code as an integer or rely on floats for exact values.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by asking what the value is and what we will do with it. If it is a yes/no answer, it is a Boolean: true or false. If it is one single character, it is a char; if it is text of any length, it is a string. If it is a number we will do math with, I pick an integer when it is always whole, like a count or age, and a float when it needs a decimal, like a height or temperature. The tradeoff is that types change behaviour: adding the strings "5" and "5" gives "55", not 10. Things that look numeric but are really labels, like ZIP codes or phone numbers, should be strings, because as integers they lose leading zeros. Also, floats are approximations, so they can show small rounding errors where exact values matter.
rubricPoints: Defines a data type as the kind of value, which controls storage and allowed operations.
Distinguishes char (one character) from string (sequence of characters).
Distinguishes integer (whole number) from float (number with a decimal part).
Describes Boolean as holding only true or false.
Names a pitfall, such as numeric-looking labels losing leading zeros as integers or floats having rounding error.

suggested.rationale: The exam skill is looking at a described piece of data and picking the right type, which is best practised through short scenario questions rather than a full hands-on mission.

lessons.plain: A program needs places to keep information and ways to organise its work. A variable is a labelled box whose contents can change, like a scoreboard during a game. A constant is a box that is sealed once filled, like the number of days in a week. An array is a row of numbered boxes holding a list of similar items. A function is a reusable recipe: you hand it ingredients, it follows the steps, and it gives back a result. An object bundles the facts about one thing together with what that thing can do, like a car with its colour, its speed and its ability to brake.
lessons.guessPrompt: A shop's program uses a sales-tax rate that never changes while the program runs, plus a running total that grows as items are scanned. Which of the two should be stored so that it cannot be changed by accident, and why?
lessons.teach:
A variable is a named storage location whose value can change while the program runs, such as score = 0 that later becomes 10. A constant is a named value that is set once and must not change, such as TAX_RATE = 0.08. Many languages write constants in capitals as a signal to other programmers. An array is a single name that holds an ordered list of values, and each value is reached by its index, a position number that usually starts at 0. A function is a named, reusable block of steps. It takes inputs called parameters and often returns an output. An object groups related data, called properties or attributes, with the actions that work on that data, called methods.

These tools work because they let you name things once and reuse them. You fix a value in one place, write logic once, and keep related data together.

Worked example: a cart. Start with the constant TAX_RATE = 0.08 and the array prices = [4, 10, 6]. The function total(prices) sets a variable subtotal = 0. It adds prices[0], so subtotal is 4. It adds prices[1], so subtotal is 14. It adds prices[2], so subtotal is 20. It then returns 20 x 1.08 = 21.60. A cart object could hold prices as a property and offer checkout() as a method that calls total.

A common mistake is forgetting that indexes start at 0. The third item is prices[2], and asking for prices[3] reaches past the end of the list. Depending on the language, a running program either crashes with an out-of-range error or quietly reads a wrong value. A second mistake is typing 0.08 in many places instead of using a constant. When the tax rate changes, one copy gets missed and totals disagree. Choosing the right tool means you can say which one a problem needs: changing data needs a variable, fixed data needs a constant, a list needs an array, repeated steps need a function, and a thing with both data and behaviour needs an object.

questions.prompt:
A small library works out late fees. It sets the constant FEE_PER_DAY = 0.25 and the array daysLate = [2, 0, 5], which holds how many days each of three books is overdue. The function fees(daysLate) sets a variable owed = 0.
Step 1: it adds daysLate[0] x 0.25, so owed is 0.50.
Step 2: [missing]
Step 3: it adds daysLate[2] x 0.25, so owed is 1.75.
It then returns 1.75.
Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: It adds daysLate[0] x 0.25 again, so owed is 1.00
It adds daysLate[2] x 0.25, so owed is 1.75
It adds daysLate[1] x 0.25, so owed stays 0.50
It replaces owed with daysLate[1] x 0.25, so owed becomes 0
questions.why: Indexes start at 0, so the second value is daysLate[1], which is 0 days. Adding 0 x 0.25 leaves owed at 0.50, and Step 3 then brings it to 1.75.

questions.prompt: A weather app shows the current outdoor temperature and updates that number every hour while the app is running. Which programming tool should hold that temperature?
choices: A constant, because it is a single named number
A function, because the value is updated regularly
A variable, because the value changes while the program runs
An array, because temperatures are numbers
questions.why: A variable is a named storage location whose value can change while the program runs, and an hourly temperature changes in exactly that way.

questions.prompt: A music streaming app needs a way to represent each song. A song should keep its title and its length in seconds, and it should also be able to perform actions such as play() and pause(). Which programming tool fits best?
choices: A constant, because a song's title does not change
An object, with title and length as properties and play() and pause() as methods
A function, because play() is a reusable set of steps
An array, because a song is a list of details
questions.why: An object groups related data (properties) with the actions that work on that data (methods), and a song has both data and behaviour.

questions.prompt: A factory program stores five sensor readings in an array named readings. A programmer wants the last reading and writes readings[5]. What is the most likely result?
choices: The program returns the first reading, because the list wraps around
The program returns the fifth reading, because there are five readings
The code reaches past the end of the list, so the program may crash with an out-of-range error or read a wrong value
The program automatically adds a sixth reading set to 0
questions.why: With indexes starting at 0, five readings sit at positions 0 to 4, so readings[5] goes past the end. Depending on the language, that causes a crash or reads a wrong value.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how variables, constants, arrays, functions and objects differ, using one small example of your own, and name one limit or tradeoff of using them.
lessons.modelAnswer: A variable is a named value that can change, like a running total. A constant is named once and stays fixed, like a tax rate, so nobody alters it by accident and there is only one place to update it. An array stores an ordered list under one name, and you reach each item by an index that usually starts at 0. In a list of three prices, the last one is index 2. A function packages steps you reuse. You pass in parameters and get a result back, for example total(prices). An object bundles data with the actions on it, such as a cart holding its prices and a checkout method. There are tradeoffs. Arrays can be read past their end if you miscount indexes, which causes crashes or wrong values. Functions and objects add structure that pays off in larger programs but can be overkill for a tiny script.
rubricPoints: Variables hold values that can change, while constants are set once and stay fixed.
An array is an ordered list reached by index, usually starting at 0.
A function is a reusable named block with parameters and an optional return value.
An object groups data (properties) with behaviour (methods).
Gives a concrete example that maps each concept to a role.
Names a limit, such as out-of-range index errors or the overhead of extra structure.

suggested.rationale: Writing a first real script makes the learner create variables, use lists and define functions, which turns these definitions into working habits.

lessons.plain: Before and while writing a program, developers use a few standard ways to organize their thinking. Pseudocode is the plan written in plain sentences. A flowchart is the same plan drawn as boxes and arrows. Object-oriented methods group related data and actions into reusable units. Branching lets a program choose between paths, and looping lets it repeat steps. Think of a cooking recipe: you jot the steps down first (pseudocode), maybe sketch them as a diagram (flowchart), say 'if the sauce is thick, add water' (branching), and 'stir until smooth' (looping).
lessons.guessPrompt: A program must check each of 500 customer records and send a reminder only to customers whose bill is overdue. Which two ideas does it need: one to repeat the work and one to make a choice?
lessons.teach:
Organizational techniques are ways of planning and structuring code so it is clear and correct. Pseudocode is an informal, plain-language description of program steps, written without strict syntax (the exact grammar rules a real programming language enforces), so anyone can read it before coding starts. A flowchart is a diagram of the same logic: ovals mark start and end, rectangles are actions, diamonds are decisions with yes/no arrows, and arrows show the order. Object-oriented methods (object-oriented programming, or OOP) organize code around objects, which bundle data (properties, also called attributes) with actions (methods); a class is the template objects are made from, and inheritance lets one class reuse another's features. Branching is code that picks a path based on a condition, a test that is true or false, usually written as if/else. Looping repeats a block of code; a for loop runs a set number of times or once per item, and a while loop runs as long as a condition stays true.

Worked example, a reminder program. Pseudocode: for each customer, if days overdue is greater than 0, send a reminder; otherwise skip. Trace it with three customers whose days overdue are 0, 12 and 3. Loop pass 1: 0 is not greater than 0, so the branch skips. Pass 2: 12 is greater than 0, reminder sent. Pass 3: 3 is greater than 0, reminder sent. The loop ends after the last item: two reminders. As a flowchart this is a decision diamond inside a loop arrow that returns to 'next customer'.

A common mistake is writing a while loop whose condition never becomes false, called an infinite loop. In a running system that program never finishes, can pin the processor at full use, and may keep sending duplicate reminders. Another mistake is confusing the two: branching chooses once, looping repeats.

questions.prompt: A shipping depot plans a labeling program in pseudocode: for each package, if weight is greater than 20 kg, label it "heavy"; otherwise label it "standard". Trace it with four packages weighing 25 kg, 20 kg, 8 kg and 31 kg. Pass 1: 25 is greater than 20, so it is labeled heavy. Pass 2: [missing step]. Pass 3: 8 is not greater than 20, so it is labeled standard. Pass 4: 31 is greater than 20, so it is labeled heavy. The loop ends after the last package, with two heavy labels. Which choice correctly fills in Pass 2?
choices: 20 reaches the 20 kg limit, so the branch labels it heavy
The condition is false for 20, so the loop stops and the last two packages are never checked
20 is not greater than 20, so the branch labels it standard
20 does not pass the test, so the package is skipped and gets no label
questions.why: The test is strictly "greater than 20", so 20 makes the condition false and the else path applies the standard label, which matches the final count of two heavy labels.

questions.prompt: A team draws a flowchart for a vending machine. One step asks "Is the inserted coin valid?" and leads to separate yes and no arrows. Which flowchart shape should this step use?
choices: A rectangle
A diamond
A plain arrow with no shape
An oval
questions.why: A diamond marks a decision, which is a true-or-false question with yes and no arrows leading out of it. Ovals mark start and end, and rectangles mark actions.

questions.prompt: A parking garage app needs a Vehicle template that stores a plate number and has a "pay fee" action. Car and Motorcycle must reuse those same features without rewriting them. Which organizational technique fits best?
choices: Object-oriented methods: make a Vehicle class, and let Car and Motorcycle inherit from it
Pseudocode: describe the vehicles in plain language, since that replaces the need for templates
Looping: use a for loop that repeats the plate-number code for each vehicle type
Branching: use an if/else to pick between car and motorcycle each time
questions.why: In object-oriented programming, a class is a template that bundles data (properties) with actions (methods), and inheritance lets other classes reuse those features.

questions.prompt: A water plant's program says: while tank level is less than 100%, run the pump. However, the code never reads a new tank level after the loop starts, so the stored level stays at 40%. What is the most likely result on the running system?
choices: The branch picks the pump path once and then moves on to the next step
The loop runs once, sees 40%, and stops because a while loop checks its condition only one time
The loop never ends, so the program never finishes and can keep the processor at full use
The program reports a syntax error before it runs, because pseudocode rules forbid this
questions.why: The condition never becomes false, which makes this an infinite loop: the program never finishes, can pin the processor at full use, and keeps repeating the action.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how pseudocode, flowcharts, OOP, branching and looping differ, and name one limit or tradeoff of at least one of them.
lessons.modelAnswer: Pseudocode and flowcharts are planning tools: pseudocode writes the logic in plain sentences, and a flowchart draws it with shapes, with diamonds for decisions and arrows for flow. Neither runs; they help people agree on logic before coding. OOP is a way to structure real code by grouping data and the actions on it into objects built from classes, which makes reuse easier through things like inheritance. Branching and looping are control flow: branching uses a true/false condition to choose a path, like if/else, while looping repeats steps, either per item or while a condition holds. A tradeoff: flowcharts are great for simple logic but become messy and hard to maintain for large programs, and pseudocode has no strict rules, so it can be ambiguous. A limit of loops is that a bad condition can create an infinite loop that never ends and wastes CPU.
rubricPoints: Pseudocode is plain-language logic with no strict syntax.
A flowchart shows logic visually, with diamonds for decisions.
OOP groups data and methods into objects created from classes.
Branching chooses a path based on a true/false condition.
Looping repeats steps, and a never-false condition causes an infinite loop.
Names a real limit or tradeoff, such as flowcharts getting unwieldy or pseudocode being ambiguous.

suggested.rationale: The exam asks learners to read a short scenario and name the right technique, so reasoning through situations, backed by the loops-and-conditions practice in python-02-log-parser, builds that skill best.

lessons.plain: Data is raw facts a business collects, such as sales receipts, website clicks or sensor readings. On its own it is like a pile of puzzle pieces: you only see the picture once you sort and assemble it. The value of data comes from turning those pieces into something useful. A company can use it to make better decisions instead of guessing, summarize it in reports so people can see what is happening, and even earn money from it by selling insights or building better products. That is why organizations treat data as an asset, something worth protecting and investing in, like equipment or cash.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small bakery records every sale: item, time and price. Without any special training, name one decision the owner could make better by looking at a month of those records.
lessons.teach:
Data is raw, unprocessed facts, such as a list of 3,000 sales lines. Information is data that has been organized and given context so a person can act on it, such as "croissants sell out by 9 a.m. on weekdays." Analytics is the process of examining data to find patterns, trends and relationships. A data-driven decision is a choice based on evidence found in data rather than on habit or gut feeling.

Reporting means presenting analyzed data in a regular, readable form: a summary table, a chart, or a dashboard (a screen of live charts and key numbers that updates as new data arrives). Reports matter because most decision makers will never read raw records; they need the meaning delivered clearly and on time.

Monetization means earning money from data. This can be direct, such as selling anonymized trend data to partners, or indirect, such as using purchase history to recommend products that raise sales, or offering a paid analytics feature to customers. Because data can drive decisions, reports and revenue, organizations call it a data asset and invest in collecting, storing and protecting it.

Worked example. A bakery owner exports a month of sales (data). Step one: group the lines by item and hour. Step two: a chart shows croissants run out at 9 a.m. while muffins are often thrown away at closing (information). Step three: a weekly report puts this in front of the owner. Step four: she bakes more croissants and fewer muffins (a data-driven decision), cutting waste and raising sales. Step five: a local supplier pays for her anonymized weekday demand trends (monetization).

A common mistake is assuming that more data automatically means better decisions.
