Inaccurate, incomplete or out-of-date data produces confident but wrong conclusions, and spotting two things that move together does not prove one causes the other. In a running business, bad data leads to wasted stock, misjudged budgets and poor products, and monetizing data carelessly can break privacy laws and lose customer trust.

questions.prompt: A city library wants to spend its yearly book budget better. Step 1: staff export twelve months of loan records, one line per checkout (data). Step 2: they group the records by title and format, and a chart shows e-book waitlists averaging six weeks while many print copies of the same titles were never borrowed (information). Step 3: a monthly dashboard, a screen of live charts and key numbers, puts these figures in front of the library director. Step 4 is missing. Step 5: a regional library network pays for the library's anonymized, title-level demand trends, with no patron names included (monetization). Which choice best completes Step 4 as a data-driven decision?
choices: The director moves part of the print budget into extra e-book licenses for the titles with the longest waitlists.
The director holds off on any change and orders another three years of records, since more data will automatically make the decision better.
The director keeps buying the same mix of print and e-books as last year, because long-time staff feel that mix has always worked.
The director sells each patron's named borrowing history to a publisher so that the publisher can target ads at them.
questions.why: A data-driven decision acts on the evidence the analysis found, here long e-book waits and unused print copies, rather than on habit, endless extra collecting, or careless monetization that would break privacy.

questions.prompt: A food-delivery company collects many kinds of records. Which of the following is information rather than raw data?
choices: "Orders from the downtown area double on rainy Friday evenings, so more drivers are needed then"
A log file of GPS coordinates recorded every ten seconds from each delivery bike
A database table that lists every driver's ID number and vehicle type
A spreadsheet with 50,000 rows, each showing an order time, an address and an order total
questions.why: Information is data that has been organized and given context so a person can act on it, and only the rainy-Friday statement does that; the other choices are unprocessed records.

questions.prompt: A music-streaming service uses each listener's play history to suggest new songs. The suggestions keep listeners engaged, so more of them renew their paid subscriptions. The company never sells the history to anyone. Which concept does this best show?
choices: Direct monetization, because the company sells data to outside partners
Raw data, because play history has not yet been analyzed in any way
Indirect monetization, because the data raises revenue without being sold
Reporting, because the play history is shown to managers in a regular summary
questions.why: Indirect monetization means using data to increase earnings, here through recommendations that drive renewals, instead of selling the data itself.

questions.prompt: A hardware store manager notices that, over the past year, weeks with high umbrella sales were also weeks with high sales of indoor paint. She concludes that displaying umbrellas causes people to buy paint, so she moves the umbrellas next to the paint aisle. What is the main problem with her reasoning?
choices: Moving products is a monetization decision, so it cannot also count as a data-driven decision.
Two things moving together does not prove that one causes the other; rainy weather could be driving both.
She should have used a dashboard instead of yearly records, because dashboards always prove cause and effect.
One year of sales lines is raw data, and raw data can never be analyzed to find patterns.
questions.why: Spotting two things that rise together does not prove one causes the other, and acting on that mistaken link can lead to confident but wrong business decisions.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how a company gets value from the data it collects through decisions, reporting and monetization, and name one limit or risk that can make that value disappear.
lessons.modelAnswer: Raw data, like individual sales records, is not very useful until we analyze it and turn it into information with context, such as which products sell best at which times. That information supports data-driven decisions, meaning we choose based on evidence instead of guessing, for example adjusting stock levels. Reporting is how that information reaches people: regular summaries, charts or dashboards that busy managers can read quickly. Monetization is earning money from data, either directly by selling anonymized insights or indirectly by using it to improve products, recommendations or paid features. Because it does all this, data is treated as a business asset. The big limit is quality: if the data is wrong, incomplete or stale, the reports and decisions will be wrong too, and a pattern in the data does not prove cause. Monetizing also carries privacy and legal risk if personal data is mishandled.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes raw data from information that has been organized and given context.
Explains a data-driven decision as a choice based on evidence rather than guesswork.
Describes reporting as presenting analyzed data clearly, such as summaries or dashboards.
Explains monetization as direct sale of insights or indirect revenue from better products.
Names a limit such as poor data quality, correlation versus causation, or privacy risk.

suggested.rationale: Turning raw CSV fleet records into a fuel-efficiency report lets the learner experience firsthand how raw data becomes information that supports a decision.

lessons.plain: A database is an organized collection of data that software can store, search and update reliably. A relational database keeps data in tables, grids of rows and columns much like a spreadsheet, and links tables together through shared identifying values. A non-relational database (often called NoSQL) stores data in more flexible shapes, such as whole documents or simple name-and-value pairs, without requiring every entry to follow the same layout. Think of a relational database as a cabinet of identical printed forms cross-referenced by ID numbers, and a non-relational one as folders of notes where each note can look different.
lessons.guessPrompt: A library records its members and the books they borrow. Every member already has a unique card number. How could the list of loans show who borrowed each book without copying the member's full name and address into every loan entry?
lessons.teach:
A relational database stores data in tables and connects them through keys. A table holds one kind of thing, such as customers. A row, also called a record, is one instance of that thing, like one customer. A field, also called a column or attribute, is one piece of information every row has, like email or city. The schema is the planned structure: which tables exist, which fields each has, and what type of data each field accepts.

A primary key is a field whose value uniquely identifies each row in its table; it can never repeat or be empty. A foreign key is a field in one table that holds a primary key value from another table, creating the link, or relationship, between them.

Worked example. A Customers table has fields CustomerID (primary key), Name and Email. Row: 101, Ana Ruiz, ana@example.com. An Orders table has OrderID (primary key), CustomerID (foreign key) and Total. Row: 5001, 101, 40.00. To find who placed order 5001, read its CustomerID, 101, then look up 101 in Customers and get Ana Ruiz. Ana's details are stored once, so changing her email updates every order's view of her. Notice that 101 may appear in many Orders rows; a foreign key does not need to be unique, only the primary key it points to does.

A non-relational database skips fixed tables. A document store keeps each item as a self-contained record, often in JSON form, and items may have different fields. A key-value store pairs a unique key with a value for very fast lookups. A graph database stores items and the connections between them. These suit fast-changing or loosely structured data and spread easily across many servers, while relational databases suit structured data needing strict consistency, like finances.

A common mistake is using something like a person's name as a primary key. Two customers can share a name, so lookups return the wrong person and orders get attached to the wrong account; a generated ID avoids this.

questions.prompt: A public library uses a relational database. Its Books table has BookID (primary key), Title and Author. One row is 3305, Tide Charts, M. Okafor. Its Loans table has LoanID (primary key), BookID (foreign key) and DueDate. One row is 7720, 3305, 2025-06-14. A librarian wants to know which book loan 7720 was for. Step 1: find the Loans row with LoanID 7720 and read its BookID, which is 3305. Step 2: ???. Step 3: read the Title from the matching row, Tide Charts. Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: Search the Loans table for every other row whose BookID is 3305 and take the earliest one
Match the DueDate 2025-06-14 against the Books table to find the book due on that date
Look up 7720 in the BookID field of the Books table, because the loan number points straight to the book
Look up 3305 in the BookID field of the Books table, where it is the primary key and matches exactly one row
questions.why: The foreign key value 3305 in Loans points to the primary key in Books, so looking up 3305 there returns the one book that was lent.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic keeps a Pets table. It has the columns PetID, Name, Species and OwnerPhone. One entry reads 88, Biscuit, Dog, 555-0142. In database terms, what is the line '88, Biscuit, Dog, 555-0142'?
choices: A schema, because it sets out the structure of the Pets table
A primary key, because it identifies Biscuit uniquely
A field, because it holds the information for one pet
A row, also called a record, because it is one instance of a pet
questions.why: A row, or record, is one instance of the thing the table holds. Here that is one pet, while the columns such as Species are its fields.

questions.prompt: A fitness app needs to store which members follow which other members. It must quickly answer questions like 'who follows the people Jordan follows?' The connections change constantly. Which kind of database best fits this data?
choices: A document store, because each member must have exactly the same fields
A graph database, because it stores items and the connections between them
A key-value store, because each member needs only one value for very fast lookups
A relational database, because strict consistency matters most for follower lists
questions.why: A graph database is built to store items together with the connections between them. That makes it a natural fit for who-follows-whom data.

questions.prompt: A small gym's Members table uses the Surname field as its primary key. Payments are linked to members through that field. Two different people named Patel join in the same month. What is the most likely result?
choices: The surname can't serve as a unique primary key, so lookups may find the wrong Patel and payments may land on the wrong account
Nothing goes wrong, because a primary key is allowed to repeat as long as the foreign key is unique
The database turns itself into a non-relational database so it can hold both Patels
Only the Payments table is affected, because foreign keys must never repeat
questions.why: A primary key must uniquely identify each row. A shared surname breaks that rule, so records can be attached to the wrong person, and a generated ID would avoid the problem.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how tables, rows, fields, primary keys and foreign keys work together in a relational database, and when you might choose a non-relational database instead, naming one tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: A relational database organizes data into tables, each holding one kind of thing. Each row is one record, and each field is one attribute every row shares, defined by the schema. Every table has a primary key, a value that is unique and never empty, so each row can be found exactly. To connect tables, another table stores that value as a foreign key; for example, an Orders table holds CustomerID so each order points to one customer, and customer details are stored only once. Foreign key values can repeat because one customer can have many orders. A non-relational database, such as a document or key-value store, drops the fixed table layout, which makes it flexible for varied or rapidly changing data and easy to spread across servers. The tradeoff is that you give up some of the strict structure and built-in relationships that keep related data consistent.
rubricPoints: Defines a table as one kind of thing, a row as one record, and a field as one attribute.
States that a primary key uniquely identifies each row and cannot be empty or repeat.
Explains that a foreign key stores another table's primary key to link the tables, and may repeat.
Describes non-relational databases as flexible formats such as document, key-value or graph stores.
Names a tradeoff, such as flexibility and scaling versus strict structure and consistency.

suggested.rationale: Building linked tables with primary and foreign keys and then joining them in a SQL lab makes the relationships concrete in a way reading alone cannot.

lessons.plain: A database is an organized store of information, and using it mostly means asking it questions and presenting the answers. A query is a precise question, such as "which customers ordered this month?" A report takes query results and arranges them into a readable summary, like a monthly sales sheet. Scalability is how well the database copes as the data and the number of users grow. Finally, the database has to live somewhere: on your own machines (local) or rented from a provider over the internet (cloud). Think of a library. A query is asking the librarian for a book, a report is the yearly reading list, and scalability decides whether you expand the building or open branches.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small shop keeps its sales database on one office computer. Sales triple and the computer slows down. Can you think of two different ways to fix this, one that changes the computer and one that adds something?
lessons.teach:
A query is a request that retrieves or changes data in a database. Relational databases, which store data in tables, are usually queried with SQL (Structured Query Language). A query names what you want, where it lives and any conditions, for example: select the name and total from the Orders table where the date is in March. A report is a formatted presentation of query results, often with totals, groupings or charts, meant for people making decisions. The query finds the data and the report presents it.

Scalability is a system's ability to handle more data, users or requests without failing or slowing badly. Vertical scaling (scaling up) means giving one server more CPU, memory or disk. It is simple, but one machine has a ceiling, and upgrades can require downtime. Horizontal scaling (scaling out) means adding more servers and spreading the work across them. It can grow much further, but it is harder to keep the data consistent across machines.

Local storage, also called on-premises, means the database runs on hardware you own. That gives you full control and keeps data in your building, but you pay up front and must maintain it yourself. Cloud storage means a provider hosts the database and you reach it over the internet. Growing is easy and you pay as you go, but you depend on the network connection and on the provider.

Worked example: a shop's single sales server is slow. Step one, the team adds memory, which is vertical scaling, and speed returns. Step two, sales grow again and the server is already at its maximum memory. Step three, they move to a cloud database that adds servers on demand, which is horizontal scaling. Their monthly report now runs the same query across the larger dataset.

A common mistake is treating a report and a query as the same thing, or assuming cloud is always cheaper. Steady, predictable workloads can cost less on local hardware.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic keeps its appointments in a relational database on one server in its back office. Step 1: a staff member asks the database for the pet name and appointment time from the Appointments table where the date is tomorrow. That request is a query. Step 2: the results are laid out as a printed daily schedule, grouped by vet, with a count of visits for each vet, so the practice manager can plan staffing. That formatted output is a report. Step 3: the clinic opens two new branches and appointment traffic grows about fivefold. The server already holds the most memory and CPU its hardware supports, and it is still slow. Step 4: ______. Step 5: the same daily schedule report now runs against the larger dataset without slowing badly. Which choice correctly fills Step 4?
choices: Install more memory in the existing server, which is vertical scaling and solves the slowdown
Add more servers and spread the work across them, which is horizontal scaling
Move to a cloud database mainly because cloud hosting is always cheaper than owning hardware
Rename the daily schedule report as a query so the database treats it as a lighter request
questions.why: The single server has reached its hardware ceiling, so adding servers and spreading the load (horizontal scaling) is how the system keeps growing.

questions.prompt: A city water department's finance manager receives a monthly document showing spending totals grouped by department, with a bar chart comparing each one. Which term best describes this document?
choices: A report, because it is a formatted presentation of query results for decision-makers
Horizontal scaling, because it combines data from several departments
A query, because it requests data from the database tables
A table, because the spending figures are stored in rows and columns
questions.why: A report presents query results in a formatted way, such as totals and charts, for people making decisions, while the query is what retrieves the data.

questions.prompt: A 20-person accounting firm runs a database with a steady, predictable workload that barely changes from month to month. A partner says, "We should move it to the cloud, because cloud is always cheaper." Which response is most accurate?
choices: Correct, because pay-as-you-go pricing always costs less than owning hardware
Correct, because cloud databases never depend on a network connection
Incorrect, because cloud storage cannot hold relational databases
Incorrect, because steady, predictable workloads can cost less on local hardware
questions.why: Cloud makes growth easy, but it is not automatically cheaper, and a stable workload can be less expensive to run on owned, on-premises hardware.

questions.prompt: A new mobile game expects its player count to grow unpredictably, possibly far beyond what any single machine can handle. Which scaling approach fits best, and what is its main trade-off?
choices: Vertical scaling (upgrading one server); it can grow without any limit
Horizontal scaling (adding servers); upgrades always require planned downtime
Vertical scaling (upgrading one server); data consistency across servers becomes harder
Horizontal scaling (adding servers); keeping data consistent across machines is harder
questions.why: Scaling out by adding servers can grow much further than one machine allows, at the cost of making data harder to keep consistent across those servers.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a query and a report, and between vertical and horizontal scaling. Then name one tradeoff of moving a database from local storage to the cloud.
lessons.modelAnswer: A query is the precise question we send to the database, for example an SQL statement asking for all orders over 100 dollars from last week. A report takes those results and formats them for people, with totals, groups or charts, so a manager can act on them. When the database gets too busy, we can scale vertically by giving the one server more CPU, memory or disk. That is simple, but it hits a hardware ceiling and may need downtime. We can also scale horizontally by adding more servers to share the load. That grows further, but it is harder to keep the data consistent. Moving from local to cloud storage makes scaling easy and turns up-front hardware costs into pay-as-you-go. The tradeoff is that we depend on the internet connection and the provider, we give up some control, and steady workloads can end up costing more over time.
rubricPoints: A query retrieves or changes specific data, often using SQL.
A report formats query results for human decision-making.
Vertical scaling upgrades one server and has a ceiling.
Horizontal scaling adds servers and grows further, but adds complexity.
Local storage gives control but has up-front cost and needs maintenance.
Cloud storage scales easily but depends on the network and provider, and is not always cheaper.

suggested.rationale: Writing real queries and turning their results into a simple report is best learned by doing, and the planned SQL lab would have the learner do exactly that.

lessons.plain: A backup is a spare copy of your data kept somewhere else so you can get it back if the original is lost. A file system backup copies files and folders, the way your computer organizes documents on a drive. Where you keep that copy matters as much as making it. A copy on the same computer is fast but disappears if the computer is stolen or burns. A copy in another building or in the cloud, meaning storage rented over the internet, survives that. It is like keeping a spare house key: one in your pocket is handy, but you also want one at a friend's place.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose your only backup is on a USB drive that stays plugged into your laptop all the time. Name two things that could destroy the laptop's files and that backup at the same moment.
lessons.teach:
A backup is a separate copy of data that you can restore, meaning copy back, after the original is lost or damaged. A file system backup copies files and folders as the operating system stores them, such as documents, photos and configuration files. The storage target is where the backup copy is saved.

There are two broad kinds of storage target. A local target is in the same place as the original. Examples are a second internal disk, an external USB drive, or a NAS (network-attached storage, a small file server on the office network). Local targets are fast to write to and fast to restore from, and they need no internet. Their weakness is shared risk: fire, theft, flood or a power surge can take out the original and the copy together. The other kind is an offsite or cloud target. Offsite means another physical location. Cloud storage means space rented from a provider and reached over the internet. These survive a local disaster, but restores are slower and depend on bandwidth and an ongoing fee.

A common guideline is the 3-2-1 rule: keep 3 copies of the data, on 2 different kinds of storage, with 1 copy offsite.

Here is a worked example. A small office stores invoices on one PC. Copy 1 is the PC itself. Each night the files are copied to a NAS, which is copy 2, on different media. The NAS then syncs to cloud storage, which is copy 3 and is offsite. If the PC's disk fails, they restore quickly from the NAS. If the office floods, they restore from the cloud.

A common mistake is treating an always-connected drive or a synced folder as a full backup. Ransomware is malicious software that encrypts files so they cannot be read. It can encrypt or delete anything the computer can reach, and a sync tool copies deletions too. Another mistake is never test-restoring. A backup that cannot be restored is worth nothing, and you often discover that only during an outage, when the data is already gone.

questions.prompt: A two-person accounting firm wants to follow the 3-2-1 rule for its client spreadsheets. Step 1: Copy 1 is the office laptop where the spreadsheets live. Step 2: Every Friday the spreadsheets are copied to an external USB drive kept in a desk drawer. That is copy 2, on a different kind of storage, but it is still local. Step 3: (missing) Result: the firm now has 3 copies, on 2 kinds of storage, with 1 copy offsite. Which action correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Copy the spreadsheets into a second folder on the laptop's own disk
Upload the spreadsheets to a rented cloud storage service over the internet
Copy the spreadsheets to a second internal disk added to the laptop
Copy the spreadsheets to a second USB drive and keep it in the same desk drawer
questions.why: Only cloud storage puts a copy in another physical location, which supplies the 1 offsite copy that the rule requires, while the other choices all keep every copy in the same office.

questions.prompt: A dental practice backs up its appointment files to a NAS (a small file server on the office network) in the same room as its main PC. It keeps no other copies. A fire destroys the room. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: Both the original and the backup are lost, because a local target shares the same physical risks as the original
The files can be restored quickly from the NAS, because local targets are fast to restore from
The NAS survives, because network-attached storage is stored in the cloud
The files are safe, because the NAS is a separate kind of storage from the PC
questions.why: A local target sits in the same place as the original, so a fire, flood or theft can destroy the original and the copy together.

questions.prompt: A freelance writer's only backup is a folder that automatically syncs every change to an online storage service. Ransomware, which is malicious software that encrypts files so they cannot be read, scrambles the files on her computer. Why might her backup fail to help?
choices: Online storage is always slower to restore from than a local drive
Cloud storage cannot be reached over the internet while ransomware is running
The sync tool copies the changes, so the encrypted versions replace the good copies online
Ransomware can only affect files stored on internal disks, not online ones
questions.why: A sync tool copies changes and deletions as they happen, so damage on the computer is passed straight to the synced copy.

questions.prompt: A charity has backed up its donor files to an external drive every night for two years, but nobody has ever tried copying the files back. What is the main risk of this habit?
choices: The drive will fill up, because backups cannot be overwritten
Untested backups are automatically deleted by the operating system
The backups will not count as copies under the 3-2-1 rule unless they are tested
If the backup turns out to be unusable, they may only find out during an outage, after the original data is already gone
questions.why: A backup that cannot be restored is worth nothing, and without test-restores this problem is usually discovered only when the data is needed and already lost.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between keeping a file backup on a local target and keeping it offsite or in the cloud. Say which risks each one protects against, and name one tradeoff or limit of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: A file system backup is a restorable copy of our files and folders, and the storage target is where that copy lives. A local target is something like an external drive or the NAS in our office. It is fast to back up and fast to restore, and it works without internet. But it sits in the same building, so a fire, theft or flood could destroy it along with the original. An offsite or cloud target is in another location, so it survives a local disaster. The tradeoff is that restoring large amounts of data over the internet is slow, and it costs a recurring fee. That is why the 3-2-1 rule mixes both: three copies, two kinds of media, one offsite. One limit applies to every target: a drive that stays connected all the time, or a synced folder, can be wiped by ransomware. And none of it counts until we have actually tested a restore.
rubricPoints: Defines a backup as a separate, restorable copy and a file system backup as a copy of files and folders.
Explains that local targets are fast and convenient but share physical risks with the original.
Explains that offsite or cloud targets survive local disasters but restore more slowly and cost money.
Mentions the 3-2-1 rule or another way of combining local and offsite copies.
Notes that always-connected or synced copies are vulnerable to ransomware and deletion, or that restores must be tested.

suggested.rationale: A disaster-recovery planner would have the learner place backup copies on local and offsite targets and then watch which copies survive each simulated failure.

lessons.plain: Security boils down to a few core goals. Confidentiality means secrets stay secret. Integrity means information is not secretly changed. Availability means things work when you need them. Together these three are called the CIA triad. Two more ideas control who gets in. Authentication means proving who you are. Authorization means deciding what you are allowed to do once you are in. Think of an office building. Showing your badge at the front desk is authentication. Your badge then opening only your own floor is authorization. Locked filing cabinets keep things confidential. Sealed envelopes protect integrity. The lights staying on keeps the building available.
lessons.guessPrompt: You log into your work email with your password, but you still cannot open the payroll folder. Is the system confirming who you are, or deciding what you may do? Which word would you guess fits each step?
lessons.teach:
Confidentiality means only the people who should see information can see it. Integrity means information stays accurate and is not changed without permission, or that any change can be detected. Availability means systems and data are there when legitimate users need them. Together these three are called the CIA triad, the three goals that every security control serves. Authentication is proving who you are, for example with a password, a code sent to your phone, or a fingerprint. Authorization is deciding what an authenticated identity is allowed to do, such as reading a file but not deleting it. Authentication always comes first, because a system cannot decide your permissions until it knows who you are.

Why this helps: naming the goal tells you which control fits. Encryption, which scrambles data so only key holders can read it, protects confidentiality. A hash is a fingerprint-like value calculated from data that changes if the data changes. A hash protects integrity. Backups and spare hardware protect availability.

Worked example: a hospital clerk starts her shift. Step 1: she enters her username and password and approves a prompt on her phone. That is authentication. Step 2: the system checks her role, which is clerk. It lets her view appointment times but not diagnoses. That is authorization, and it also supports confidentiality. Step 3: an attacker alters a dosage in a record. The stored hash no longer matches, so the change is flagged. That is integrity at work. Step 4: a flood of fake traffic, called a denial-of-service attack, knocks the scheduling site offline. Availability is lost, even though nothing was read or changed.

Common mistake: treating authentication and authorization as the same thing. Logging in successfully does not mean you may do everything. Imagine a system that checks identity but then gives every user full access. It has authentication without real authorization. Any stolen low-level account then becomes a key to everything. In a running system, the safe practice is least privilege, which means giving each account only the permissions its job needs.

questions.prompt: A school runs an online gradebook. Trace what happens during one week. Step 1: a maths teacher types her password and scans her fingerprint. The system now knows who she is, so this is authentication. Step 2: the system checks her role. It lets her edit grades for her own maths classes but blocks her from changing grades in other teachers' classes. Step 3: a student sneaks into the database and changes a test score. The stored hash for that record no longer matches the recalculated one, so the change is flagged. That is integrity. Step 4: a power fault crashes the main server, and a spare server takes over within minutes so teachers can keep working. That protects availability. Which security concept is at work in Step 2?
choices: Availability, because the teacher can still reach the classes she needs
Authentication, because the fingerprint scan was a second proof of who she is
Authorization, because the system is deciding what an already identified user may do
Integrity, because blocking edits keeps other teachers' grades accurate
questions.why: Step 2 happens after her identity is proven and limits which actions she may take, which is exactly what authorization means.

questions.prompt: A delivery company sets up its staff laptops so that all files on the drive are encrypted. If a laptop is left on a train, a stranger who finds it cannot read the customer addresses stored on it. Which security goal does this control mainly protect?
choices: Availability, because the files stay on the laptop
Authentication, because the stranger has no password
Confidentiality, because only key holders can read the data
Integrity, because the stranger cannot change the addresses
questions.why: Encryption scrambles data so only people with the key can read it, which keeps the information confidential.

questions.prompt: An online shop makes every employee sign in with a password and a phone code, and that check works correctly. However, once signed in, every account, including a summer intern's, can issue refunds and delete products. An attacker tricks the intern into revealing his login and empties the shop's refund budget. What is the main weakness, and what practice fixes it?
choices: Authentication is too weak; add a third sign-in factor so stolen logins stop working
Integrity is missing; add hashes so refunds can be detected later
Availability is missing; keep backups so deleted products can be restored
Authorization is effectively missing; apply least privilege so the intern's account gets only the permissions his job needs
questions.why: Identity was checked properly, but every account had full access, so the fix is real authorization using least privilege.

questions.prompt: A software maker publishes an installer on its website and, next to it, a hash value calculated from the original file. A user downloads the installer, calculates its hash, and finds it does not match the published value. What does this tell the user, and which security goal does the check serve?
choices: The user is not allowed to install it, so authorization has failed
Someone else may have read the file, so confidentiality has been broken
The download was too slow, so availability has been lost
The file has been changed since it was published, so the check protects integrity
questions.why: A hash changes whenever the data changes, so a mismatch reveals alteration, which is what integrity protection detects.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says, 'If users log in with strong passwords, our data is secure.' Explain to them, in your own words, the difference between authentication and authorization and the three CIA goals. Name one tradeoff or limit, such as a case where adding protection for one goal can hurt another.
lessons.modelAnswer: A strong password only covers authentication, which is proving who someone is. After that, authorization decides what that person may do. Without limits, any stolen account could read or delete everything, so we should give each account least privilege. Security also has three goals, called the CIA triad. Confidentiality keeps data visible only to the right people, for example through encryption and access rules. Integrity makes sure data is not changed without detection, for example with hashes. Availability keeps the system usable when people need it, for example with backups and redundancy. Logging in well does nothing to stop a denial-of-service attack taking the site down. The tradeoff is that controls can pull against each other. Very strict lockouts after a few failed logins protect confidentiality, but an attacker can deliberately lock out real users. That harms availability, so we have to balance the controls.
rubricPoints: Authentication is proving identity, and it happens before authorization.
Authorization decides what an authenticated user is allowed to do, ideally with least privilege.
Confidentiality means only the right people can see data.
Integrity means data is not changed without permission or detection.
Availability means systems and data work when legitimate users need them.
Names a real tradeoff, such as strict security controls reducing availability or convenience.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this by giving short scenarios and asking which concept applies, so practicing classification of realistic situations builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Device security means protecting a single computer, phone, or tablet from harm. Think of the device as a house. Anti-malware is the guard who checks visitors for known troublemakers. A firewall is the front door that only opens for expected guests. Patching is fixing broken windows before burglars notice them. Physical security is locking the house so nobody carries it away. Safe browsing is choosing not to invite strangers in. Each protection stops a different kind of trouble, so you use them together. When something goes wrong, the useful question is which specific weakness was exploited and which protection covers it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A coworker leaves a laptop unlocked on a café table, and it is stolen. Which would have helped most: anti-malware software, a firewall, or a screen lock plus a cable lock?
lessons.teach:
Device security is the set of controls that protect one endpoint. An endpoint is any device a person uses directly, such as a laptop or phone. A control is a specific protective measure. The key skill is matching each threat to the control that actually addresses it.

Malware is harmful software. It includes viruses, ransomware (which locks your files and demands payment), and spyware. Anti-malware software scans files and running programs. It compares them against signatures, which are fingerprints of known malware, and it also watches for suspicious behavior. A firewall filters network traffic using rules. It allows or blocks connections based on things like the port, which is a numbered doorway that a network service listens on. A vulnerability is a flaw that an attacker can exploit. A patch is an update that fixes a flaw, so patching closes known holes in the operating system and in applications. Physical security protects the hardware itself. Examples are cable locks, locked rooms, and automatic screen locks. Safe browsing means habits that avoid web threats. You check that a link goes where it claims to go, refuse unexpected downloads and pop-ups, and install only trusted browser extensions (add-ons that run inside the browser). Phishing is a fake message that tricks you into clicking a link or giving up details.

Worked example: a user opens an email attachment called invoice.exe. First, ask how the threat arrived. It came through a user action, so safe-browsing and email habits are the first defense. Second, ask what would catch the file. Anti-malware can block it if it matches a signature or behaves suspiciously. Third, ask what weakness it would use. If it exploits an unpatched flaw, patching would have closed that path.

A common mistake is thinking one control covers everything. A firewall does not stop malware that the user willingly downloads through allowed web traffic. Delaying updates is a second mistake, because attackers actively target flaws that have publicly known fixes. On a running system, an unpatched machine can be taken over and used to attack others on the same network. Layered controls, where each one covers a different path, are the reliable approach.

questions.prompt:
Priya runs a two-person bakery and uses one laptop for orders. An IT volunteer matches each of three problems to the control that addresses it.

Problem A: Priya often leaves the laptop open on a café table while she orders coffee. Matched control: physical security. A cable lock holds the laptop to the table, and an automatic screen lock after 1 minute hides her screen. This works because the threat is someone touching or taking the hardware itself.

Problem B: The operating system has shown an update notice for 3 months. The update fixes a publicly known flaw. Matched control: patching. Installing the update closes that known hole, and attackers actively target flaws like this.

Problem C: The laptop's log shows repeated connection attempts from the internet to port 3389. Port 3389 is a remote-access service that Priya never uses. Matched control: ______

Which control completes Problem C?
choices: Anti-malware, because it compares the incoming connections against signatures of known viruses
A cable lock, because it stops outsiders from reaching the laptop
A firewall rule that blocks incoming connections on port 3389, because a firewall allows or blocks traffic by port
A trusted browser extension, because it filters the traffic that reaches the browser
questions.why: The threat is unwanted network traffic aimed at a specific port, and a firewall is the control that filters connections by rules such as port number.

questions.prompt: In anti-malware software, what is a signature?
choices: A numbered doorway that a network service listens on
A rule that allows or blocks a network connection
An update that fixes a flaw in the operating system
A fingerprint of known malware that scanned files are compared against
questions.why: Anti-malware detects known threats by comparing files and programs against signatures, which are fingerprints of known malware.

questions.prompt: At a veterinary office, receptionists often walk away from the front-desk computer for several minutes. A pet owner could read client records on the screen while it is unattended. Which control most directly addresses this threat?
choices: Installing the latest operating system patch
Running a full anti-malware scan every night
Setting an automatic screen lock after a short idle time
Adding a firewall rule that blocks unused ports
questions.why: The threat is a person physically viewing the unattended device, so a physical security control such as an automatic screen lock addresses it.

questions.prompt: A warehouse company's firewall allows normal web traffic. An employee visits a file-sharing site and willingly downloads a free tool, which secretly contains spyware. Why did the firewall not stop it?
choices: The download used allowed web traffic, and the user started it, so a firewall alone does not cover this path
The spyware exploited an unpatched flaw that the firewall had not yet been told about
The firewall needed a newer signature list to recognize the spyware
Firewalls only protect against physical theft of the hardware
questions.why: A firewall filters traffic by rules, and allowed web traffic that the user willingly downloads passes through, so other layers such as safe browsing and anti-malware must cover it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a laptop needs anti-malware, a firewall, patching, physical security, and safe-browsing habits all together, and name one limit of any single control.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each control covers a different way in. Anti-malware scans files and programs for known signatures or suspicious behavior. Its limit is that brand-new malware may not match any signature yet. A firewall filters network connections by rules, such as which ports are allowed. However, it lets through traffic that looks permitted, like a download the user chose to make. Patching fixes known vulnerabilities in the OS and apps, but it only works if updates are actually installed, and it cannot fix flaws nobody has found yet. Physical security, such as screen locks, cable locks, and locked rooms, stops theft and someone sitting down at an unlocked machine, which no software prevents. Safe browsing covers the human path, for example not clicking phishing links or installing unknown extensions. Because every control has gaps, we layer them so one covers another's blind spot.
rubricPoints: Defines each control by what it specifically does.
Matches controls to threats, such as phishing to safe browsing and theft to physical security.
States a concrete limit, such as a firewall not stopping user-chosen downloads or signatures missing new malware.
Explains that patching closes known vulnerabilities and that delaying updates is risky.
Concludes that layered controls cover each other's gaps.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing the right control for a described situation, so reasoning through short device scenarios builds that matching skill better than any current mission.

lessons.plain: A password is a secret word or phrase that proves you are the owner of an account. Good password practices make that secret hard to guess and limit the damage if it ever leaks. Use long passwords, mix character types, keep them private, and never use the same one twice. A password manager is an app that creates and remembers a unique password for every account. Think of a key ring: you would not use one key for your house, car and office. If someone copied it, they could open everything.
lessons.guessPrompt: Which do you think is harder for a computer to guess by trying every combination: an 8-character password using letters, numbers and symbols, or a 16-character password made only of lowercase letters?
lessons.teach:
A password practice is a habit that makes a password hard to guess and limits damage if it leaks. Length is the number of characters. Complexity means mixing character types: lowercase, uppercase, digits and symbols. Privacy means the password stays secret. You do not share it, write it on a sticky note, or type it where others can watch. Reuse means using the same password on more than one account, and you should avoid it. A password manager is an app that generates long random passwords and stores them in an encrypted vault, which is a locked, scrambled store. It also fills them in for you, so you only memorize one master password, the key to the vault.

Why it works: attackers often use brute force, which means trying every possible combination. The number of combinations is the number of available characters raised to the power of the length. Each extra character multiplies the attacker's work.

Worked example. Step 1: eight lowercase letters give 26 to the 8th power, about 209 billion combinations. Step 2: keep eight characters but allow all 94 keyboard characters. That gives 94 to the 8th, about 6 quadrillion, roughly 29,000 times harder. Step 3: instead use sixteen lowercase letters. That gives 26 to the 16th, about 44 sextillion, millions of times harder than step 2. Length added more than complexity did. That is why a long passphrase, several random words strung together, is a strong choice.

Common mistake: reusing one strong password everywhere, or making predictable swaps like P@ssw0rd. Attackers already know those swaps. Reuse also enables credential stuffing. That is when attackers take username and password pairs leaked from one breached site and try them automatically on many others.

Consequence: if a reused password leaks from a small forum, an attacker can log into your email. From there, they can use password-reset links to take over your other accounts. A unique password per account keeps the damage to one site.

questions.prompt: A cycling club's smart bike locks use a PIN made only of digits (0 to 9, so 10 possible characters). The club wants to know how much a longer PIN helps against brute force, meaning an attacker trying every possible combination. Step 1: a 4-digit PIN gives 10 to the 4th power, which is 10,000 combinations. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: compare the two. The 6-digit PIN is 100 times harder to brute-force, even though only two characters were added. Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: A 6-digit PIN gives 6 to the 10th power, about 60 million combinations.
A 6-digit PIN gives 10,000 times 2, which is 20,000 combinations, because two digits were added.
A 6-digit PIN gives 10 to the 6th power, which is 1,000,000 combinations.
A 6-digit PIN gives 10,000 plus 2 extra digits' worth, about 10,020 combinations, because each new digit adds 10.
questions.why: Combinations equal the number of available characters raised to the power of the length, so 10 characters at length 6 is 10 to the 6th, or 1,000,000, which is 100 times the 4-digit total.

questions.prompt: A small online knitting forum is breached, and its list of usernames and passwords is leaked. Within hours, an automated tool tries those exact username and password pairs on banking, shopping and email sites. What is this attack called?
choices: Brute force
Complexity attack
Password manager vault cracking
Credential stuffing
questions.why: Credential stuffing means taking username and password pairs leaked from one site and automatically trying them on many other sites, which only works when people reuse passwords.

questions.prompt: A receptionist at a dental clinic must pick a new login password for the scheduling system. Based on how brute force works and what attackers already know, which choice is the strongest?
choices: Summer2024! (eleven characters following a common pattern)
D3nt@l!2 (eight characters with letter-to-symbol swaps)
Xq7! (four characters using all four character types)
lantern oyster gravel pickle (four random words strung together)
questions.why: A passphrase of several random words is long, and length multiplies the attacker's work far more than complexity does, while predictable swaps and patterns are already known to attackers.

questions.prompt: Priya uses a password manager, an app that creates long random passwords and keeps them in an encrypted vault. Every site password is unique and long. However, she has written her master password, the one key to the vault, on a sticky note attached to her office monitor. Which password practice is she failing?
choices: Length, because a master password can never be long enough to protect a vault.
Complexity, because the sticky note removes the mix of character types.
Privacy, because the master password is not kept secret and anyone nearby can read it.
Reuse, because the master password is used for more than one account.
questions.why: Privacy means the password stays secret, and writing the master password on a visible sticky note exposes the key to every password in the vault.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why you recommend long, unique passwords stored in a password manager instead of one complex password they memorize and reuse. Name one limit or tradeoff of the approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Attackers guess passwords by brute force, trying combinations. The count of combinations grows with the number of character types, but it grows much faster with length. That is because each added character multiplies the possibilities. So a long passphrase usually beats a short password with symbols, and predictable swaps like @ for a do not help much. Reuse is the bigger danger. When one site is breached, attackers try the leaked username and password on other sites, which is called credential stuffing. A single reused password could hand them your email and then everything else through password resets. A password manager solves this by generating and remembering a unique random password for every account. You also keep passwords private: never share them or leave them written where others can see. The tradeoff is that the manager becomes one high-value target. Its master password must be long, unique and never shared, because losing it exposes or locks you out of everything.
rubricPoints: Length increases guessing difficulty more than complexity alone because each character multiplies the combinations.
Complexity means mixing character types, but predictable substitutions add little protection.
Reusing a password lets one breach spread to other accounts through credential stuffing.
Passwords must stay private: not shared, written down openly, or typed where others can see.
A password manager generates and stores unique passwords so only one master password must be remembered.
Tradeoff: the manager's master password becomes a single point of failure and must itself be strong and unique.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing the right password practice for a described account or scenario, so reasoning through exam-style situations builds that judgment best, and no current mission or planned engine practices it directly.

lessons.plain: Encryption scrambles information with a secret key so that anyone without the key sees only gibberish. Think of it like a lockbox: the contents are useless to a thief unless they also have the key. Data needs this protection in two situations. When it sits stored on a laptop, phone, or server, that is data at rest. When it moves across a network, such as from your browser to a website, that is data in transit. Each situation needs its own lock, because protecting one does not protect the other. HTTPS and VPNs protect data while it moves. Device encryption protects data while it is stored.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your laptop is stolen from a café, and separately you log in to your bank over the café's public Wi-Fi. Do you think the same protection keeps both situations safe, or does each need a different kind of lock? Why?
lessons.teach:
Encryption turns readable data, called plaintext, into scrambled data, called ciphertext, using a mathematical process and a key. A key is a secret value that locks and unlocks the data. Without the right key, ciphertext is useless, which is why encryption protects confidentiality, meaning only intended people can read the data.

Data at rest is data stored on a disk, USB drive, phone, or server. Full-disk encryption encrypts the entire drive, so a stolen device reveals nothing unless the thief also has the password or key that unlocks it. Modern phones usually encrypt their storage automatically once you set a screen lock, such as a PIN, password, or biometric. The lock is what protects the key, so a phone with no PIN gives little real protection.

Data in transit is data moving across a network. HTTPS is web traffic (HTTP) wrapped in TLS, which stands for Transport Layer Security. TLS encrypts traffic between your browser and the website and uses a certificate, a digital ID card, to prove the site's identity. A VPN, or virtual private network, builds an encrypted tunnel from your device to a trusted network, so everything you send passes through that tunnel. This matters most on untrusted networks like public Wi-Fi.

Worked example: you upload a report from café Wi-Fi to a company HTTPS site. Step one: on your laptop the file is at rest, protected by full-disk encryption. Step two: as it travels, TLS encrypts it, so others on the Wi-Fi capture only ciphertext. Step three: on the company server it is at rest again, and only the server's own storage encryption protects it there.

A common mistake is assuming the HTTPS padlock means the site is safe or that your data stays protected forever. The padlock only means the connection is encrypted. A scam site can have one too, and data on the server is not covered by HTTPS. In a running system, protecting only one state leaves a gap: an encrypted connection to a server with unencrypted disks still exposes everything if those disks are stolen.

questions.prompt: A delivery driver for a florist keeps customer addresses and signature photos on a company phone. The phone is left in a taxi and never recovered. The driver's manager reasons it through. Step 1: The addresses and photos are stored on the phone, so they are data at rest. Step 2: The phone encrypts its storage automatically, but that encryption only helps if a screen lock protects the key that unlocks it. Step 3: The driver never set a PIN, password, or biometric, so anyone holding the phone can open it and read everything. Step 4 is missing: what should the florist require on every company phone to close this gap?
choices: Require a VPN app on every phone so all stored data stays inside an encrypted tunnel
Nothing more, because the phone's automatic storage encryption already protects it
Require a screen lock, such as a PIN, password, or biometric, on every phone
Require staff to only open websites that show the HTTPS padlock
questions.why: A phone's storage encryption gives real protection only when a screen lock guards the key, so setting a lock is what protects data at rest on a lost phone.

questions.prompt: A shopper finds an unfamiliar online store selling headphones at 80% off. The address bar shows the HTTPS padlock. What does that padlock actually tell the shopper?
choices: The shopper's whole device is now sending all traffic through an encrypted tunnel
The connection between the browser and the site is encrypted, but the store could still be a scam
The store is legitimate and has been checked as safe to buy from
The shopper's card details will stay encrypted on the store's servers forever
questions.why: HTTPS uses TLS to encrypt the connection only; a scam site can have a padlock too, and HTTPS does not cover data stored on the server.

questions.prompt: A sales rep waiting at an airport joins the free public Wi-Fi and needs to use email, a chat app, and the company's internal file share. She wants everything her laptop sends over this untrusted network to be encrypted to her company's trusted network. Which control fits best?
choices: Full-disk encryption on the laptop
Setting a stronger screen-lock password
Checking that one website shows the HTTPS padlock
Connecting through the company VPN
questions.why: A VPN builds an encrypted tunnel from the device to a trusted network so all traffic passes through it, which is what matters on public Wi-Fi.

questions.prompt: A small accounting firm's client portal uses HTTPS, so uploads are encrypted as they travel. Its file server, however, has no storage encryption. One night burglars steal the server. What is the result?
choices: The client files can be read, because data at rest on the server was never encrypted
The client files are safe as long as the firm's website certificate is still valid
The client files can be read only if the burglars also connect over public Wi-Fi
The client files are safe because HTTPS encrypted them when they were uploaded
questions.why: HTTPS protects data only in transit; once stored on unencrypted disks, the data at rest is exposed if those disks are stolen.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between protecting data at rest and data in transit, which tool fits each (full-disk or device encryption, HTTPS, VPN), and name one thing each protection does not cover.
lessons.modelAnswer: Encryption scrambles data with a key so that only someone who has the key can read it. Data at rest is stored data, on a laptop, phone, or server. We protect it with full-disk or device encryption, so a stolen device gives up nothing. That protection depends on a strong lock like a PIN or password, and it does nothing once the data leaves the device. Data in transit is data crossing a network. HTTPS uses TLS to encrypt traffic between a browser and one website, and its certificate proves the site's identity. A VPN encrypts all of your traffic in a tunnel to a trusted network, which is useful on public Wi-Fi. The limit is that both only protect the trip. The padlock doesn't mean the site is honest, and once data lands on the server, only that server's own at-rest encryption protects it. You need both kinds of protection.
rubricPoints: Defines encryption as scrambling data with a key so only key holders can read it.
Distinguishes data at rest (stored) from data in transit (moving over a network).
Matches full-disk or device encryption to data at rest, and explains it depends on a screen lock or password.
Matches HTTPS (TLS) and VPNs to data in transit, and notes a VPN covers all traffic through a tunnel.
Names a limit, such as the padlock not proving a site is trustworthy, or in-transit protection not covering stored data.

suggested.rationale: The exam skill is picking the right encryption for a given situation, so working through short scenarios like a stolen phone, public Wi-Fi, or a web login builds that judgment best.

scenarios.title: First Week at Larkfield Outdoor Supply
scenarios.scenario:
Nadia has just started as a junior support technician at Larkfield Outdoor Supply, a fictional camping-gear shop with one store and a small warehouse. Her lead, Priya, gives her a short briefing and then four tasks.

Priya's briefing: Every computer job follows four stages. Input is data going into the system, such as a key press or a barcode scan. Processing is the CPU (central processing unit, the chip that carries out instructions) working on that data. Output is the result coming back out, such as text on a screen or a printed page. Storage is where data is kept for later, such as on an SSD (solid-state drive, a storage device with no moving parts). A CPU's speed is often given as clock speed, measured in hertz (Hz), meaning cycles per second. MHz (megahertz) is one million cycles per second, and GHz (gigahertz) is one billion. So 1 GHz equals 1,000 MHz.

Computers count in binary, a base-2 notational system (a way of writing numbers) that uses only the digits 0 and 1. In an 8-digit binary number, the place values from left to right are 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. You add up the place values wherever there is a 1. Decimal is the everyday base-10 system with the digits 0 to 9. Hexadecimal, or hex, is base 16. It uses the digits 0 to 9 and then the letters A to F, where A=10, B=11, C=12, D=13, E=14 and F=15. Each hex digit stands for exactly four binary digits, so you can split an 8-digit binary number into two halves of four and convert each half on its own. Within a group of four, the place values are 8, 4, 2 and 1.

A bit is one binary digit, and a byte is 8 bits. Storage is usually measured in bytes. For example, MB means megabyte, GB means gigabyte, and TB means terabyte. For this job, treat 1 GB as 1,000 MB. Network throughput (how much data moves per second) is usually measured in bits per second. Mbps means megabits per second, and Gbps means gigabits per second. The lowercase b means bits, and the uppercase B means bytes. A very common beginner mistake is to mix up the two. That makes a transfer look 8 times faster than it really is, which leads to missed deadlines and wrong promises to users.

The troubleshooting method Larkfield uses has these steps, in order: identify the problem (ask the user questions and find out what changed), establish a theory of the likely cause, test the theory, make a plan and implement the solution, verify full system functionality, and document the findings, the actions taken and the outcome.

The tasks:

1. At the till, a cashier scans a tent's barcode. The till's 2.4 GHz CPU looks up the price and adds it to the total. The total appears on the screen and is printed on the receipt, and the sale is saved to the till's SSD. Name which part of this is input, processing, output and storage. Then state what 2.4 GHz measures and give the same value in MHz.

2. A setting on the warehouse network switch is shown as the binary value 10101100. Convert it to decimal and to hexadecimal, and show your working.

3. Nadia must copy a 2 GB backup of the sales records to the office server over a 100 Mbps link. Ignoring any overhead, work out how many seconds the copy will take, and explain why simply dividing 2,000 by 100 gives the wrong answer.

4. Yesterday the label printer at the packing desk stopped printing. Nadia's colleague Omar guessed that its cable was loose. He pushed the cable back in, printed one test page, and then closed the support ticket with no notes. Which troubleshooting steps did Omar carry out? Which steps did he skip? Explain one problem his shortcut could cause later.
modelAnswer: Input: the barcode scan of the tent. Processing: the 2.4 GHz CPU looking up the price and adding it to the total. Output: the total shown on the screen and printed on the receipt. Storage: the sale being saved to the SSD. 2.4 GHz is the CPU's clock speed, meaning 2.4 billion cycles per second. Because 1 GHz = 1,000 MHz, it is 2,400 MHz.

Decimal: the 1s in 10101100 sit at the place values 128, 32, 8 and 4. Adding them gives 128 + 32 + 8 + 4 = 172. Hex: split the number into two groups of four, 1010 and 1100. 1010 = 8 + 2 = 10, which is A in hex. 1100 = 8 + 4 = 12, which is C in hex. So the answer is 172 in decimal and AC in hexadecimal.

The file size is in bytes, but the link speed is in bits per second, so convert first. 2 GB = 2,000 MB, and each byte is 8 bits, so 2,000 MB × 8 = 16,000 megabits. Then 16,000 megabits ÷ 100 Mbps = 160 seconds (about 2 minutes 40 seconds). Dividing 2,000 by 100 gives 20 seconds. That mixes megabytes with megabits and ignores the factor of 8, so the copy would look 8 times faster than it really is.

Omar loosely identified the problem: he knew the printer had stopped, but he did not ask the user questions or find out what changed. He established a theory (a loose cable), tested it and implemented the fix in one move by reseating the cable and printing one test page. He skipped verifying full system functionality. For example, he did not print real shipping labels from the order system, so he does not know that normal work actually runs again. He also skipped documenting his findings, actions and outcome in the ticket. Possible consequences: the real problem may still be there, or if it comes back, the next technician has no record of the symptom, cause or fix. They have to start from scratch, and nobody notices that the same cable keeps working loose.

scenarios.title: Setting Up a New Hire's Desk at Brightwell Kitchen Supply
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Brightwell Kitchen Supply, a fictional 20-person company that sells restaurant equipment, as a junior IT technician. Your manager, Dana, asks you to get a new sales coordinator, Luis, ready for his first day. Here is what you find.

Luis's laptop has 4 GB of RAM (random access memory, the short-term working memory the computer uses for programs that are open right now) and a 512 GB SSD (solid-state drive, long-term storage with no moving parts). He keeps about 30 browser tabs and a spreadsheet open, and the laptop slows down badly whenever he switches between them. The storage is only one-third full.

Luis's desk is next to the break room, which has a microwave. When the microwave runs, his Wi-Fi (wireless networking based on the IEEE 802.11 family of standards) drops out. The office Wi-Fi uses the 2.4 GHz band, a radio frequency range that many household appliances also use. There is an unused network jack in the wall under his desk, and a cable from that jack runs to a box in the wiring closet with 24 numbered ports. A separate box in the closet connects the office to the internet provider.

Dana also gives Luis a shared office printer. Windows sees that 'a device' is connected by USB (Universal Serial Bus, a common plug-in cable connection), but it is listed as 'Unknown device' and will not print.

Finally, Brightwell wants a new customer-tracking application. The vendor runs the software on its own servers, handles all updates, and staff simply log in through a web browser.

Your tasks:
1. Name the internal component you would upgrade to fix the slowdown, and explain why upgrading storage would not help.
2. Give a wired fix for the Wi-Fi dropouts. Name the interface Luis's laptop would use and the component inside the laptop that provides it, and name the device in the closet with 24 ports and the device that connects the office to the internet.
3. Explain what is missing for the printer and how you would fix it.
4. Identify the cloud service model for the customer-tracking application and explain how it differs from IaaS.
modelAnswer: Upgrade the RAM, for example from 4 GB to 8 GB or 16 GB. RAM is volatile memory, meaning it holds data only while the power is on, and it is where open programs and browser tabs are kept while they are in use. When RAM fills up, the computer pushes some of that work onto the much slower storage drive, and that causes the lag Luis sees when he switches between tabs. Storage is non-volatile, meaning it keeps files even when the power is off, and it holds saved files rather than running programs. His SSD is only one-third full, so more storage space would not change how much work he can keep open at once. A common mistake is to buy a bigger drive here: the money is spent and the slowdown stays.

Plug a network cable from the wall jack into the laptop's Ethernet port. Ethernet is the standard wired network connection and uses a cable with an RJ45 plug. The port is provided by the NIC (network interface card), the laptop component that connects it to a network. Every NIC has a MAC address, a fixed hardware ID used to deliver data on the local network. A wired cable is not affected by radio interference from the 2.4 GHz microwave. The 24-port box in the closet is a switch. A switch connects devices within the same LAN (local area network, the network inside one building or site) and sends traffic to the correct port using MAC addresses. The box that connects the office to the internet provider is a router. A router moves traffic between different networks, such as the office LAN and the WAN (wide area network, a network that spans large distances, like the internet), using IP addresses. An acceptable alternative is moving Wi-Fi to the 5 GHz band, but the task asks for a wired fix.

The printer is missing its driver. A driver is small software that tells the operating system how to talk to a specific piece of hardware. Windows can see that something is attached over USB, but without the driver it does not know what the device is or how to send it print jobs, so it shows 'Unknown device'. The fix is to download the correct driver for that exact printer model and operating system from the printer manufacturer, install it, then confirm the printer appears by name and print a test page. A common mistake is to keep unplugging the cable or swapping USB ports. That does not solve a missing driver, and Luis still cannot print.

This is SaaS (Software as a Service). The vendor hosts and maintains the complete, ready-to-use application, and users simply log in through a browser. Brightwell manages no servers or software installation. IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) is different because the provider supplies only the basic building blocks, such as virtual servers, storage, and networking, usually running on a hypervisor (software that runs several virtual machines on one physical computer). With IaaS, the customer would still have to install, update, and manage the operating system and the application. So with SaaS, Brightwell is responsible for the least: user accounts and its own data.

scenarios.title: First Week on the Help Desk at Larkspur Garden Supply
scenarios.scenario:
You have just started as a junior help desk technician at Larkspur Garden Supply, a fictional company that sells plants and tools from three shops and one office. Your team lead, Dana, gives you four tickets to handle before lunch. For each one, name the specific part of the system or the specific feature that solves the problem, not just 'use an app' or 'restart it.'

Some background Dana shares with you. A file system is the method an operating system (the core software that runs a computer, such as Windows) uses to organize and store files on a drive. FAT32 (File Allocation Table, 32-bit) is an older file system that almost every device can read, but it cannot store any single file larger than 4 GB. NTFS (New Technology File System) is the modern Windows file system. It handles very large files and supports file permissions, which are rules about who may open or change a file. A driver is a small piece of software that tells the operating system how to talk to a specific piece of hardware, such as a printer. A browser cache is a store of copies of web pages and images that the web browser (the program used to view websites) saves on the computer so pages load faster next time. Private browsing is a browser mode that does not save history, cookies (small files websites store to remember you), or form entries on that computer once the window is closed. Generative AI is software that creates new text or images by predicting which content is most likely to come next, based on patterns in the data it learned from.

Ticket A: Marco in marketing has a 6 GB promotional video. He tries to copy it to a USB drive he uses on Windows computers. The copy fails with 'file too large,' even though the drive shows 20 GB free. The drive is formatted as FAT32.

Ticket B: After a Windows update last night, the office printer no longer prints. The printer powers on and its own test page prints fine, but nothing sent from the computer comes out.

Ticket C: The shops share a front-counter computer. A cashier, Priya, needs to log in to her personal bank website on her break. She does not want her login or history left behind for the next person. Separately, the store manager says the company's own website still shows last week's prices on that computer, even though the web team confirms the prices were updated.

Ticket D: The office manager used a generative AI chatbot (a program you talk to by typing questions) to draft a returns policy. The draft says customers have 90 days to return items, but Larkspur's real limit is 30 days. She asks why the tool would 'lie.'

1. For Ticket A, explain why the copy fails and name the file system change that fixes it.
2. For Ticket B, name the OS component most likely at fault and what you would do.
3. For Ticket C, name the browser feature for Priya and the browser feature that fixes the old prices.
4. For Ticket D, explain why the chatbot produced the wrong number and what the manager should do.
modelAnswer: The copy fails because FAT32 cannot store any single file larger than 4 GB. The amount of free space does not matter: the 6 GB video is over the per-file limit. The fix is to reformat the USB drive as NTFS, which supports very large files and works on Windows computers. Marco must first copy anything he needs off the drive, because reformatting erases the drive. The worked logic: the file is 6 GB, the FAT32 limit is 4 GB, 6 is greater than 4, so the copy fails no matter how much space is free. A common mistake is assuming 'file too large' means the drive is full and buying a bigger FAT32 drive, which still fails.

The most likely fault is the printer driver, the software that lets the operating system talk to the printer. The printer works on its own because its test page prints, so the hardware is fine. The break is between the computer and the printer, and that started right after an OS update, which can replace or break a driver. The fix is to update or reinstall the correct printer driver. A common mistake is replacing the printer or its cables when the hardware is not the problem.

For Priya, use private browsing. It does not keep her history, cookies, or form entries on the shared computer after she closes the window. Mentioning that she should still log out and close the private window strengthens the answer. A good answer may also note that private browsing only hides activity on that computer, not from the network or the website. For the old prices, clear the browser cache. The browser is showing a saved copy of last week's page instead of downloading the updated one. Clearing the cache forces it to fetch the current page. A common mistake is assuming the website itself is broken when only the local saved copy is out of date.

Generative AI creates text by predicting which words are most likely to come next, based on patterns in the data it learned from. It does not know Larkspur's actual policy. A number like 90 days is a common return period elsewhere, so the tool predicted it as a likely answer. It is not lying on purpose; it produced plausible-sounding content that happens to be wrong. The manager should treat the draft as a starting point only, check every fact against the real company policy, correct the limit to 30 days, and have a person review it before publishing. If she publishes it unchecked, customers could rely on the wrong return period.

scenarios.title: Planning the Order Tracker at Brightloaf Bakery
scenarios.scenario:
Brightloaf Bakery is a small, fictional bakery that takes custom bread orders. Priya, a new junior developer, is planning a simple order-tracking program before she writes any code. Her team lead, Marcus, asks her to name the exact building blocks the program needs, not just to say she will write some code.

Each order record holds five pieces of information. The first is the customer's first initial, such as M. The second is the customer's full name, such as Maria Okafor. The third is the number of loaves ordered, such as 14. The fourth is the price per loaf in dollars, such as 4.75. The fifth is whether the order has been paid, which is either yes or no.

The program also has some rules. A sales tax rate of 0.08 (8 percent) applies to every order and must never change while the program runs. The program must keep a list of all of today's order totals together so it can add them up at closing time. Any order of more than 12 loaves gets a 10 percent discount, and smaller orders do not. The program must check this discount rule for every order in today's list, one after another, until it reaches the end of the list.

Finally, the bakery's public menu page will be built in HTML (HyperText Markup Language). HTML is used to describe how text and images are laid out on a web page. The checkout logic will be written in Python, a language that a separate program reads and runs one line at a time, with no separate step to turn the whole program into machine code first.

A data type is the kind of value a piece of data holds, and it tells the computer how to store and use that value. Answer Marcus's questions below.

1. Name the most suitable data type for each of the five pieces of information in an order record: the first initial, the full name, the number of loaves, the price per loaf, and the paid status. Give a one-line reason for each.
2. Name the programming concept that should hold the 0.08 tax rate, and the programming concept that should hold the list of today's order totals. Explain why each one fits.
