3. Name the organizational technique that applies the 10 percent discount only to orders over 12 loaves, and the technique that repeats the discount check for every order in the list. Explain what each does.
4. Classify the type of language used for the menu page and the type of language used for the checkout logic. Explain the difference in how each is used.
subParts: Data types for the order record
modelAnswer: The first initial should be a char (character). A char holds exactly one letter, digit, or symbol, and M is a single character. The full name should be a string. A string is a sequence of characters, and Maria Okafor is many characters including a space. The number of loaves should be an integer. An integer is a whole number with no decimal part, and you cannot order part of a loaf. The price per loaf should be a float (floating-point number). A float is a number that can have a decimal part, and 4.75 has cents. The paid status should be a Boolean. A Boolean holds only one of two values, true or false, which matches paid yes or no. A common mistake is storing the price as an integer. The cents would be dropped, so 4.75 becomes 4 and every total comes out wrong.

The tax rate should be a constant. A constant is a named value that is set once and cannot be changed while the program runs. The rule says 0.08 must never change, so a constant protects it from being altered by accident. A variable would be the wrong choice here. A variable is a named storage location whose value can change during the program, so it would allow the rate to be changed in error. The list of order totals should be an array. An array is a single named structure that holds many values of the same type in order, each reached by its position. An array keeps all of today's totals together, so the program can go through them and add them up at closing time.

Applying the discount only to orders over 12 loaves uses branching. Branching is a decision point where the program checks a condition and follows one path if it is true and another if it is false. Here the logic is: if loaves is greater than 12, apply the 10 percent discount; otherwise, charge the normal price. For example, an order of 14 loaves takes the discount path, and an order of 6 loaves takes the normal path. Repeating the check for every order uses looping. Looping means running the same set of steps again and again, here once per order in the array, until a stopping point is reached, which is the end of the list. A common mistake is writing the check only once. Then only the first order is checked, and every other order is charged incorrectly.

The menu page uses a markup language (HTML). A markup language describes the structure and layout of content, such as headings, paragraphs, and images on a web page. It does not perform logic like calculations or decisions, so it is not used to run the checkout rules. The checkout logic uses an interpreted language (Python). In an interpreted language, another program called an interpreter reads and runs the code one line at a time each time it runs. A compiled language is different: the whole program is translated into machine code ahead of time, before it runs. A Python script like this is often also called scripting, meaning a short program that automates a task. The key difference is that markup only describes how content is laid out, while the interpreted Python code actually carries out the steps and decisions.

scenarios.title: Organizing Orders and Backups at Juniper Hollow Tea Company
scenarios.scenario:
Juniper Hollow Tea Company is a small fictional online shop that sells loose-leaf tea. For three years the owner, Priya, has tracked everything in one large spreadsheet. Each sale is typed on its own line, and the customer's name and email are retyped every time that customer orders. The spreadsheet now has errors. Some customers appear with two different emails. Two different customers are both named "Sam Lee", so nobody can tell their orders apart. You have just joined as a junior IT assistant, and Priya wants your help.

Here are the terms you will need. A database is an organized collection of data that software can search and update. A relational database stores data in tables. A table is a grid holding one kind of thing, such as customers. Each row in a table is one record, meaning one single item, such as one customer. Each field, also called a column, is one piece of information about every record, such as an email address. Tables are linked to each other using keys. A primary key is a field whose value is unique for every row, so it identifies exactly one record. A foreign key is a field in one table that holds a primary key value from another table, which links the two records. A non-relational database (often called NoSQL) does not require a fixed table layout. It stores flexible items, such as documents or simple key-and-value pairs, and each item can have different fields. A query is a request that asks the database for specific data, for example "all orders from March". A report is a formatted summary built from query results, so that people can read it and make decisions.

Priya's plan is to split the data into two tables. The Customers table would have the fields CustomerID, Name, and Email. The Orders table would have the fields OrderID, CustomerID, OrderDate, TeaName, and Amount. Every order is always recorded with these same fields.

Priya also wants a safety copy of the new database files each night. A file system backup is a copy of selected files and folders, saved to a separate place called a storage target. A local storage target is a device kept on site, such as an external hard drive in the office. An offsite or cloud storage target is a location somewhere else, such as a rented online storage service run by another company and reached over the internet. The office is a single room above a shop, and it flooded once before.

1. Should Juniper Hollow use a relational or a non-relational database for this customer and order data? Give one reason based on the data described.
2. In Priya's two-table design, name the primary key of each table, and name the foreign key and the table it sits in. Explain how this fixes the "two Sam Lees" problem.
3. Priya wants to know which tea sold the most last quarter, so she can decide what to restock. Describe the query you would run and how a report would help her.
4. Recommend where the nightly file system backup should be stored, either locally, offsite/cloud, or both, and justify your choice using the office's situation.
subParts: Query and report for a decision
modelAnswer: Use a relational database. The data is structured and consistent: every customer has the same three fields, and every order always has the same five fields. That fits fixed tables with rows and fields well. The data also naturally splits into two related kinds of things, customers and orders, and relational tables link these through keys. A non-relational database is better suited to data whose shape varies from item to item, which is not the case here. A common mistake is choosing non-relational just because it sounds more modern. That would give up the built-in linking between customers and orders that this shop actually needs.

The primary key of the Customers table is CustomerID. The primary key of the Orders table is OrderID. The foreign key is CustomerID inside the Orders table, because it holds a value that points to one row in the Customers table. Each Sam Lee gets a different CustomerID, for example 104 and 217. Each of their orders stores that number instead of the name. So even though the names match, every order links to exactly one customer. As a bonus, each customer's email is stored only once, which stops the duplicate-email errors. A common mistake is using Name as the primary key. Names are not unique, so the database could not tell the two customers apart.

Run a query on the Orders table that selects only the orders whose OrderDate falls within last quarter. Group those orders by TeaName and add up the Amount for each tea, or count how many times each tea was ordered. Then sort the results from highest to lowest, so the top-selling tea appears first. Next, turn those results into a report, such as a simple table or chart, so Priya can read it at a glance. This is a data-driven decision: she restocks based on actual sales instead of guessing. That reduces the risk of running out of popular teas or overbuying slow sellers.

Store the backup in both places, and at minimum make sure one copy is offsite or in the cloud. A local external drive is fast to restore from and is under Priya's control. But it sits in the same room as the original data. If the office floods again, as it has before, or suffers a fire or theft, the original and the backup could be lost together. An offsite or cloud copy survives a disaster at the office. Keeping both gives quick everyday restores from the local copy and protection from a site-wide disaster through the offsite copy. A common mistake is keeping the only backup on a drive next to the computer it protects. That backup fails in exactly the situation where it is needed most.

scenarios.title: Securing a Small Office at Maple Hollow Bakery Supply
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Maple Hollow Bakery Supply, a fictional 25-person company that sells baking equipment to cafes. The office manager, Dana, asks you to review four problems she noticed this week. Before you start, here are the terms you will need.

The CIA triad is a set of three security goals. Confidentiality means only the right people can see information. Integrity means information stays accurate and is not changed without permission. Availability means information and systems are there when people need them. Authentication is proving who you are, for example by typing your password. Authorization is what you are allowed to do after you have proved who you are, such as read-only access versus permission to edit.

A strong password is long (at least 12 to 16 characters, because each extra character makes guessing far harder) and complex (it mixes upper and lower case letters, numbers and symbols). It is kept private (never shared or written on a sticky note) and never reused across accounts, because if one site leaks it, attackers try the same password everywhere else. A password manager is an app that creates and stores a different strong password for each account behind one master password. Many password managers can also fill passwords in for you.

Encryption scrambles data so that only someone with the right key can read it. Data at rest is data stored on a device, such as files on a laptop drive. Full-disk encryption protects the whole drive, so a thief who removes it sees only scrambled data. Data in transit is data moving across a network. HTTPS encrypts traffic between a web browser and a website, and browsers usually show it with a padlock icon and an address starting with https://. A VPN (virtual private network) creates an encrypted tunnel from your device to the company network, even over untrusted Wi-Fi. Physical security means protecting the hardware itself, for example with locked doors or a cable lock that ties a laptop to a desk.

Here are the four problems Dana found.

First, a sales rep named Theo uses the password Summer2024 for both his company email and the payroll website. He keeps it on a sticky note under his keyboard.

Second, the company laptops hold customer contact lists and price agreements. They are often left on desks overnight in an office that gets shared cleaning crews. None of the drives are encrypted.

Third, Theo often works from coffee shops using their free public Wi-Fi. He opens files on the company's internal file server, and he logs into the company's ordering website.

Fourth, a new intern logged in with her own correct username and password. She was then able to edit the master price list. She accidentally changed several prices to zero, and the wrong prices went out to customers.

Your tasks:
1. Recommend specific password practices that fix Theo's situation, and explain why each one helps.
2. Name the controls that protect the customer data on the office laptops if one is stolen, and say whether this protects data at rest or data in transit.
3. Explain how Theo should protect his connection when working on coffee shop Wi-Fi, for both the file server and the ordering website.
4. For the intern incident, state whether the failure was in authentication or authorization, and which part of the CIA triad was harmed.
subParts: Secure remote work on public Wi-Fi
modelAnswer:
Theo's password is too short and too predictable. It is a common word plus a year, so it is easy to guess. He should switch to long passwords of at least 12 to 16 characters, because every extra character greatly increases the number of guesses an attacker needs. The passwords should also be complex, mixing upper and lower case letters, numbers and symbols, so they are not simple dictionary words.

He must stop reusing one password for email and payroll. Each account needs its own unique password, so that a leak of one does not unlock the other. He should remove the sticky note and keep passwords private, because anyone walking past his desk can read the note.

The practical fix is a password manager. It generates and stores a unique strong password for each account, so Theo only has to remember one strong master password. A good answer names at least length, complexity, no reuse, privacy, and a password manager.

The main control is full-disk encryption on every laptop. If a laptop is stolen, the thief cannot read the customer lists or price agreements without the key. This protects data at rest, meaning data stored on the device.

A second control is physical security, such as cable locks or locking laptops in a cabinet or locked room overnight. This makes theft harder in the first place.

The consequence of skipping encryption is that one stolen laptop becomes a breach of confidentiality for every customer on it. An answer that names encryption but calls it data in transit, or only says 'be careful', is incomplete.

Public Wi-Fi is untrusted, so anyone else on it may try to watch the traffic. Theo's data here is data in transit.

For the internal file server, he should connect through the company VPN first. The VPN creates an encrypted tunnel from his laptop to the company network, so others on the cafe Wi-Fi cannot read his files.

For the ordering website, he should make sure the address starts with https:// and that the padlock icon shows before logging in. HTTPS encrypts the traffic between his browser and the site, so his password and order details are not sent in readable form. He should not enter credentials on a site that shows no HTTPS.

Both answers are about encrypting data in transit. Mentioning that the VPN also covers the website is acceptable, but the answer should include HTTPS for the website.

Authentication worked correctly. The intern proved who she was with her own valid username and password.

The failure was in authorization. Her account was allowed to edit the master price list, when an intern should have had read-only access at most. The fix is to give her account fewer permissions, granting only what her role needs.

The part of the CIA triad that was harmed is integrity, because the price data was changed without proper permission and became inaccurate. Customers then received wrong prices. Confidentiality was not the main issue, because nobody unauthorized viewed secret data. Availability was not the main issue either, because the list was still accessible.
